text: Reserved APL-inspired operators AIX reserves a vocabulary for experimenting with array-oriented syntax, but reserving a glyph is not an implementation or roadmap claim. Reserved glyph Conventional inspiration only ⍴ shape/reshape ⍳ index generation ¨ each/map ∘ composition/outer product ↑ , ↓ take/drop ⍋ , ⍒ grade up/down ∊ membership/enlist ∪ unique/union ∑ , ∫ , ∂ aggregate/calculus-inspired operations The lexer emits these as symbolic-operator tokens. The parser then raises a located error explaining that the operator is unsupported. No elementwise, shape, reduction, Arrow, or IRx lowering semantics are assigned yet. This explicit rejection prevents programs from silently receiving semantics borrowed from APL or another array language. Each operator needs a documented type rule, ASTx representation, and IRx lowering before it becomes executable.

text: AIX toy grammar This EBNF describes the subset accepted by the current recursive-descent parser. Newlines are ordinary whitespace; ; can separate statements. program ::= separator* item* EOF ; item ::= metadata_block? definition separator* ; metadata_block ::= "κ" "⟦" metadata_content "⟧" ; definition ::= function_definition | constant_definition ; function_definition ::= "∴" identifier parameter_block return_clause? block ; constant_definition ::= "∴" identifier ":" type "≔" expression "∎"? ; parameter_block ::= "⟦" parameter_list? "⟧" ; parameter_list ::= parameter ("," parameter)* ","? ; parameter ::= identifier ":" type ; return_clause ::= ("→" | "->") type ; block ::= statement* "∎" | "{" separator* statement_list? "}" ; statement_list ::= statement (separator+ statement)* separator* ; separator ::= ";" ; statement ::= return_statement | conditional_return | binding | assignment | emit | expression ; return_statement ::= "⊢" expression ; conditional_return ::= "⊢" expression "⇒" expression ; binding ::= "⌁" identifier (":" type)? "≔" expression ; assignment ::= identifier "≔" expression ; emit ::= "⟣" expression ; expression ::= precedence-climbing binary expression ; unary ::= ("-" | "¬") unary | postfix ; postfix ::= primary call_suffix* ; call_suffix ::= "⟦" argument_list? "⟧" ; argument_list ::= expression ("," expression)* ","? ; primary ::= integer | float | string | boolean | "∅" | identifier | "(" expression ")" ; The expression operators and primitive spellings are listed in syntax.md . Some tokens recognized by the lexer are deliberately outside this grammar and produce explicit unsupported-feature errors.
title: AIX toy grammar

text: AIX: a toy symbolic-language experiment AIX is a small project built for fun while exploring Unicode-heavy symbolic syntax on top of ASTx and IRx. It is not a primary ArxLang product, supported language, or committed roadmap item. distribution: airx Python import: aix CLI: aix source files: .aix What currently works The toy implementation includes a Unicode lexer, limited parser, token/AST/LLVM inspection, and native backend handoff for its documented subset. Its grammar and semantics can change freely. ∴ fib ⟦ n:ℕ ⟧ → ℕ ⊢ n ≤ 1 ⇒ n ⊢ fib⟦n - 1⟧ + fib⟦n - 2⟧ ∎ ∴ main ⟦⟧ → ∅ ⟣ fib⟦10⟧ ∎ Implemented forms include function and constant definitions, typed parameters, local bindings, return and conditional-return statements, output, scalar literals and operators, explicit block terminators, and metadata blocks that are parsed then ignored. APL-inspired symbols such as ⍴ , ⍳ , ¨ , ↑ , and ↓ are reserved. The lexer recognizes them, but the parser reports that their semantics are not yet implemented. Explore locally aix --help aix --show-tokens program.aix aix --show-ast program.aix aix --show-llvm-ir program.aix aix --run program.aix There is no product or compatibility commitment. In particular, AIX does not define the Tensor, DataFrame, Series, or RecordBatch syntax promoted by the main Arx and IRx documentation. text: AIX toy syntax reference AIX is a Unicode-first, indentation-insensitive toy frontend. Whitespace and newlines improve readability, but ∎ or {...} determines function block boundaries. The grammar is an experiment and can change freely. Definitions ∴ begins a top-level definition. A function places typed parameters in semantic brackets and may declare a return type: ∴ add ⟦ left:ℤ, right:ℤ ⟧ → ℤ ⊢ left + right ∎ Omitting → type produces a unit-returning function. A top-level constant uses : and ≔ instead of a parameter block: ∴ answer:ℕ ≔ 42 ∎ Statements Form Current meaning ⊢ value Return value ⊢ condition ⇒ value Return value when condition is true ⌁ name:T ≔ value Create a mutable typed local binding ⌁ name ≔ value Create a mutable local with literal inference when available name ≔ value Assign an existing local ⟣ value Print a value through the shared ASTx/IRx print node expression Expression statement The conditional-return form builds an if with no else ; it is not a general conditional statement. Blocks and separators Pretty form ends with ∎ : ∴ main ⟦⟧ → ∅ ⟣ "hello" ∎ Compact form uses braces and optional semicolons: ∴main⟦⟧→∅{⌁x:ℕ≔41;⟣x+1} Calls and expressions Function calls also use semantic brackets: add⟦1, 2⟧ . Parentheses group expressions but do not call functions. Supported operators, from lower to higher precedence: ∨ ∧ = , == , ≠ , != , < , > , ≤ , >= , ≥ , <= , ≡ , ≅ + , - * , × , / , % ^ (right associative) Unary - and ¬ are supported. ≡ and ≅ currently lower to equality. Types and literals AIX spelling Current ASTx type ℕ , ℤ Int64 ℝ Float64 𝔹 Boolean ∅ NoneType i8 , i16 , i32 , i64 corresponding signed integer u8 , u16 , u32 , u64 corresponding unsigned integer f32 , f64 corresponding float bool , boolean Boolean str , string String ℂ is tokenized as a primitive type but intentionally rejected because the current IRx backend has no complex-number lowering. Literals include decimal integers and floats, single- or double-quoted strings, ⊤ / true , ⊥ / false , and ∅ . Line comments begin with ⍝ . Unicode identifiers are normalized to NFC by the lexer. Metadata κ⟦...⟧ introduces a balanced metadata block before a definition: κ⟦ι: hello.v1, χ: example⟧ ∴ main ⟦⟧ → ∅ ⟣ "metadata parsed" ∎ The parser currently accepts and skips metadata content; it does not attach it to ASTx or IRx output. Reserved, not implemented Index brackets ⟬...⟭ , field access, λ , tuple brackets ⟨...⟩ , ranges, and the APL-inspired operators documented separately are lexed or reserved but do not have parser/backend semantics.

text: Native Apache Arrow Support Apache Arrow is the storage and interoperability foundation for ArxLang's data-oriented runtime. IRx implements the integration in native C++ and exposes it to generated LLVM through an opaque C ABI. Architecture Arx collection syntax or IRx API -> ASTx collection nodes -> IRx semantic analysis and lowering -> IRx runtime feature activation -> generated LLVM calls irx_arrow_* / irx_rb_* symbols -> native Arrow C++ arrays, tensors, tables, and RecordBatches This boundary provides three useful properties: LLVM IR does not reproduce Arrow container layouts or ownership rules. Native runtime artifacts are compiled and linked only when a module needs them. Arrow C Data and Arrow IPC provide interoperable boundaries instead of a project-specific serialization format. Arx is Arrow-first, not Arrow-exclusive : supported scalar operations should prefer Arrow Scalar/compute where they implement Arx semantics, with LLVM/custom implementations for unsupported contracts. Control flow, classes, lists and files retain native language semantics. M0 does not yet change the existing scalar backend. The M0 architecture decision records representation, version, numerical and approval gates. The proposed imported scalar/Series stdlib.math.sqrt is not implemented by this baseline. IRx installs pyarrow and arx-arrowcpp-sources as runtime dependencies. They provide PyArrow interoperability plus the Arrow C++ headers, sources, library locations, and linker metadata used by native builds. Implemented layers Layer Native representation Current capability Array runtime Arrow arrays behind opaque irx_arrow_* handles Build, inspect, import/export, null metadata, readonly buffer views Tensor runtime arrow::Tensor Fixed-width numeric construction, shape/stride metadata, indexing, shallow views DataFrame runtime arrow::Table Static nullable/temporal columns; runtime schemas preserve RecordBatch-supported Arrow types Series runtime arrow::ChunkedArray Typed column views selected from DataFrames RecordBatch runtime arrow::RecordBatch and Arrow IPC Schemas, builders, nullable values, IPC/CSV streams, Parquet files, PyArrow round trips Arx tensors and DataFrames Arx exposes the native runtime without exposing Arrow implementation types in the language syntax: fn first(grid: tensor[i32, 2, 2]) -> i32: return grid[0, 0] fn rows() -> i32: frame: dataframe[id: i32, score: f64] = dataframe({ id: [1, 2, 3], score: [0.5, 0.8, 1.0], }) scores: series[f64] = frame.score return cast(frame.nrows(), i32) Current tensor constraints: element types: i8 , i16 , i32 , i64 , f32 , and f64 variables, fields, and return types require a static shape tensor[T, ...] is supported for runtime-shaped parameters rank-one runtime-shaped parameters support checked numeric-sequence indexing; general runtime shape calculus and returns remain restricted Arrow-backed tensor storage is readonly in the current phase Current DataFrame constraints: static columns: numeric, Boolean, string and temporal types; nullable T | none constructor input: equal-length list-literal columns matching a static schema access: frame.name or frame["name"] when the schema is statically known metadata: nrows() and ncols() runtime-schema dataframe[...] locals, parameters and returns preserve RecordBatch-supported Arrow types/metadata through checked RecordBatch conversion; they do not provide unchecked static column access Array interoperability The lower-level IRx array runtime supports: signed and unsigned 8-, 16-, 32-, and 64-bit integers float32 , float64 , and Boolean arrays explicit array-builder and handle lifecycles Arrow C Data copy import, move/adopt import, and export null count and validity-bitmap inspection readonly irx_buffer_view projection for byte-addressable fixed-width arrays Boolean values are bit-packed in Arrow and therefore do not use the generic byte-addressable buffer-view bridge. RecordBatch IPC and PyArrow The Python API in irx.record_batch is backed by a standalone native Arrow C++ shared library. It supports: signed/unsigned integers, float32 , float64 , and bool utf8 and large_utf8 date32 , date64 second, millisecond, microsecond, and nanosecond timestamps time32 and time64 units nullable fields and null values Arrow IPC streams in files and in-memory buffers The test suite verifies both directions of interoperability: IRx-written IPC is read by PyArrow, and PyArrow-written IPC is read by IRx. The direct Python API builds a fingerprinted native shared library on first use. To pre-warm that cache explicitly: python -c "from irx.builder.runtime.record_batch import ensure_record_batch_shared_library; ensure_record_batch_shared_library()" Generated IRx programs use the runtime-feature system instead; their required native artifacts are collected during the normal build/link flow. Deliberate boundaries Native Arrow support does not yet imply a complete Arrow product surface. The current implementation does not provide: an Arx query language or Arrow Compute kernel API dedicated RecordBatch syntax (use stdlib.arrow classes instead) general nested scalar access, dictionary, decimal, or arbitrary extension types mutable Tensor storage or a NumPy-compatible tensor algebra API automatic zero-copy guarantees for every import/export path These limits keep ownership, semantics, and compiler lowering explicit while the public APIs mature. Compiled Arx interoperability ( stdlib.arrow ) stdlib.arrow exposes runtime-schema RecordBatches without changing the language grammar or converting them to statically typed DataFrames. It reuses the irx_rb_* implementation; the small irx_rb_api_* facade checks statuses before reading output slots and supplies scoped class-owned handles. The frontend only binds ASTx opaque types and native capabilities for the reserved bundled module. IRx performs normal class, call, FFI, ownership analysis and lowering. Importing unrelated standard-library modules does not activate the RecordBatch runtime. Build requirements and demonstrations Use the normal Arx development environment, including Clang, a C++20 compiler, PyArrow and arx-arrowcpp-sources . Native sources are compiled on demand through the existing runtime feature registry. The executable must be able to load the Arrow shared library used at link time; it does not start Python to serialize or deserialize data. The Python peer needs PyArrow; the demonstration runner also uses the compiler to build the Arx programs. From the repository root: python examples/arrow/run.py --directory .tmp/arrow-demo # Or choose --scenario files, --scenario c, or --scenario tcp. The runner uses temporary build/output paths chosen by --directory and ephemeral loopback ports . Its examples are also integration-test inputs: examples/arrow/write_file.x creates integer, floating-point and Boolean columns in compiled Arx and writes arx.arrow . Python uses pa.ipc.open_file and checks the schema and every value. examples/arrow/read_file.x reads python.arrow , created by Python with pa.ipc.new_file , and checks the full schema and every value. A separate test supplies a mismatched schema and requires failure. examples/arrow/tcp.x sends or receives two distinct RecordBatches . The runner builds real Arx launchers and exchanges standard IPC streaming bytes with a Python process over TCP in both directions. examples/arrow/types.x exercises every scalar append/get family, schema inspection, nullable values, empty batches, builder reuse and repeated close. examples/arrow/component.x builds a shared native component. Python invokes component__produce_stream / component__produce_array , then imports their outputs using PyArrow's _import_from_c APIs. The producing Arx locals have already been destroyed. The reverse functions consume PyArrow-exported data. This is compiled Arx, not the irx.record_batch Python wrapper. Public API ``` title: Write a RecordBatch ``` import (Schema, BatchBuilder, RecordBatch, IPCWriter) from stdlib.arrow fn main() -> i32: schema: Schema = Schema() schema.add("id", "int64") schema.add("score", "float64") schema.add("active", "bool") builder: BatchBuilder = BatchBuilder(schema) builder.append_i64(0, 42) builder.append_f64(1, 1.5) builder.append_bool(2, true) batch: RecordBatch = builder.finish() writer: IPCWriter = IPCWriter(schema) writer.open_file("example.arrow") writer.write(batch) writer.close() return 0 Schema.add(name, type_name, nullable=false) accepts validated scalar names: Arrow scalar names Arx append/get suffix int8 , int16 , int32 , int64 i8 , i16 , i32 , i64 uint8 , uint16 , uint32 , uint64 Preserve/forward; no unsigned scalar getter float32 , float64 , bool f32 , f64 , bool utf8 , large_utf8 (also string , large_string ) utf8 date32[day] , date64[ms] date ( i64 count) timestamp[s] , timestamp[ms] , timestamp[us] , timestamp[ns] timestamp ( i64 count) time32[s] , time32[ms] , time64[us] , time64[ns] time ( i64 count) Numeric native IDs are not arguments to Schema.add ; complex schemas are imported from Arrow or read from Parquet. Types, units, timezones, nullability and metadata survive snapshots and IPC/C exports. Scalar builders/getters do not provide recursive construction or traversal. Class Operations Schema() add , nfields , name(col) , type(col) , type_name(col) , nullable(col) , equals(other) BatchBuilder(schema) append_<suffix>(col, value) , append_null(col) , finish() RecordBatch() Empty output holder; nrows , ncols , schema , is_null(col,row) , get_<suffix>(col,row) IPCReader() open_file(path) , open_stream(path) , connect(host,port,timeout_ms=30000) , next() , batch() , schema() IPCWriter(schema) open_file(path) , open_stream(path) , connect(host,port,timeout_ms=30000) , write(batch) All five classes have idempotent close() and automatic destruction at their last class reference. finish() resets the builder's column buffers for reuse; it does not destroy the builder. next() returns false only at end of stream, not for an empty batch. batch() returns an independent batch snapshot and is valid only after a successful next() . A reader's schema can be inspected before reading any batches. equals and write compare metadata as well as types and nullability. Close readers/writers before reopening them. Use open_file for the Arrow random-access file format , and open_stream for streaming format stored at a path . Both support multiple batches. Zero-field builders produce zero rows; imported zero-column batches retain their original row count. For nullable data, test is_null before a getter. Typed getters reject nulls and wrong types rather than inventing default values. Arx str cannot represent embedded NUL: getters reject such text explicitly; IPC and C sharing still preserve string values without conversion. Field names and timestamp timezone strings containing NUL can round-trip through IPC, but C schema export rejects them rather than silently truncating them. Arx operations use ARX-RUNTIME-ARROW-001 on failure and terminate the process, consistent with the current File API. No source location is invented for native failures (line/column are zero). Native embedding callers needing recoverable errors should use the status-returning irx_rb_* ABI, inspect irx_record_batch_errmsg() immediately, and never read output slots on error. Same-process C Data and C Stream The native header irx_record_batch.h provides schema/batch export and move import, batch-to-stream export, and reader-to-stream export/import. It reuses irx_arrow_c_abi.h . Arrow C++ supplies the standard get_schema , get_next , get_last_error and release callbacks. No Arrow C++ layouts appear in LLVM. The pre-existing array C Data copy/move APIs remain available unchanged. Arx additionally provides: batch.export_c(array_address, schema_address) -> i32 batch.export_stream(stream_address) -> i32 batch.import_c(array_address, schema_address) reader.import_stream(stream_address) These addresses are trusted, same-process pointers encoded as i64 for the current 64-bit native targets. They are not serialized handles. Allocate zero-initialized standard structs in the host, keep their outer storage alive, and check export status before importing into PyArrow. Arbitrary addresses are unsafe. native_handle() is a borrowed opaque FFI escape hatch, not a transferable owner; never destroy it, wrap it in a second owning object, or use it after the class closes. Normal Arx code does not need this method. Exports retain Arrow buffers independently of the producing handle. Importing moves C ownership; after any attempted import, call a release callback only if it is still non-null. Import failures may already have consumed inputs. Native irx_rb_c_{array,schema,stream}_release helpers guard repeated release attempts on still-allocated outer structs , not on freed pointers. Raw opaque-handle release functions still free once and must not be called twice. irx_rb_stream_reader_export transfers the remaining iteration to the C stream; the original reader becomes exhausted and may be closed. Schema and array outputs outlive the stream. An array with release == NULL denotes end of stream; an empty batch has a live release callback. Stream callbacks are not thread-safe: serialize calls. Keep the producer shared library loaded until all exported objects have been released. RecordBatch C exports/imports share or adopt buffers without serialization; schema descriptors and wrapper objects allocate. IPC serializes data, socket reads allocate per-message buffers, and the existing buffer-input API copies its input. Existing array copy APIs also copy. These are not universal zero-copy guarantees . See the standard C Data and C Stream contracts. Across machines The Python peer listens and Arx connects, in either data direction. To move the loopback demonstration across hosts, run the Python listener on the receiving host (bind to its chosen interface), and compile the generated Arx launcher with that host's numeric IPv4 or IPv6 address and agreed port instead of loopback. Use send when Python reads with pa.ipc.open_stream(socket_file) , or receive when Python writes with pa.ipc.new_stream(socket_file, schema) . Close the Arrow writer before closing the socket so it emits the end marker. The runner's tcp() contains the complete Python peer and launcher implementation. Transport is separate from serialization ( irx_arrow_transport.* ). Native irx_rb_fd_reader_open / irx_rb_fd_writer_open duplicate a borrowed POSIX file descriptor, allowing host-supplied files/pipes as streaming endpoints. Closing these streams does not close the caller's descriptor; offsets are shared. For pipe writes, the host must arrange its SIGPIPE policy. TCP writes suppress SIGPIPE and handle partial writes, interrupted calls and connection failures. TCP is blocking, POSIX-only, numeric-address-only, with a positive connect and per-I/O timeout. It buffers messages/batches rather than an entire unbounded stream. This is not an untrusted network service : there is no authentication, TLS, batch-size quota, hostname resolution, listener API in Arx, or Flight. Use trusted peers and network controls. A slow peer can extend total transfer time by making progress; the timeout is not a whole-transfer deadline. Interop stream readers require an explicit Arrow end marker, even though some Arrow implementations accept transport EOF in its place. This detects a connection cut exactly between batches as well as truncated messages. Both PyArrow's normal writer close and the Arx writer emit this marker. A future Flight adapter can feed the same opaque batches/readers without changing the public data representation; Flight authentication and RPC are not part of this transport. Compatibility and limitations Capability Status Standalone Arx ↔ PyArrow IPC files and streams Implemented, multiple/empty batches Nullable numeric/Boolean, UTF-8 and temporal batches Runtime-schema API; checked typed methods Full field/schema metadata and timestamp timezone preservation IPC, C sharing and runtime-schema DataFrames; static casts use declared metadata Zero-column input with nonzero rows Preserved C Data/C Stream, both directions Standard structs; explicit ownership transfer TCP, both directions POSIX blocking clients; trusted numeric-address peers DataFrame ↔ RecordBatch conversion Checked exact scalar schemas, including nullable, unsigned, string and temporal columns Dictionary, decimal, binary and supported extensions Recursive C Data/IPC and Parquet forwarding; see format-specific limits Unsigned and supported nested values Forwarding supported; Arx scalar access/construction limited as above Arbitrary metadata editing, timestamp timezone creation in Arx Not exposed; imported schemas retain them Memory safety Functional ownership tests and a sanitizer harness; no blanket guarantee The sanitizer harness is packages/irx/tests/native/arrow_interop.cpp . Compile it with irx_record_batch.cpp , irx_arrow_transport.cc , irx_arrow_runtime.cc , the Arrow and buffer-native include/link flags, and -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer . It exercises schema snapshots, exported lifetimes, import moves, repeated guarded releases, EOF, CSV and checked table conversions, and corrupt-input cleanup. Pass a workspace-local CSV output path as its single argument. Arrow's prebuilt shared library itself is not sanitizer-instrumented by this command. CSV streaming and checked conversion CSVStream in stdlib.csv and Python irx.record_batch reuses Arrow C++ streaming readers and writers. Python generic stream factories remain supported. Both cast(batch, dataframe[name:T, ...]) and cast(frame, RecordBatch) support exact static scalar schemas, including nullable columns. Literal-ellipsis dataframe[...] preserves runtime schemas with rich types and metadata. Conversion results own their references independently; DataFrame-to-RecordBatch export combines all chunks and may allocate. See CSV files and DataFrames for schemas, null rules, lifetime, streaming failure semantics and the intentionally restricted DataFrame subset. Explicit CSV and Parquet streams CSVStream and ParquetStream expose open_read , open_write , batch operations, schema and close , with one active session per owner. Parquet uses Arrow's native batch reader and buffered writer, not a whole-file Table or Python subprocess. The runtime owns the parent Parquet reader across C stream exports and checks footer finalization. Supported recursive types retain Arrow metadata; unsupported types and implicit temporal coercion are rejected. See Parquet files and DataFrames for the precise contract. The record_batch runtime links libarrow ; the dependent parquet feature adds the Parquet/Dataset/Compute/Acero libraries and format adapters. Use the registered feature artifacts and linker flags for native builds. The Python ctypes backend loads Parquet as a separate on-demand plugin. Arx analyzes all stdlib.arrow declarations but lowers only resolved reachable declarations; CSV-only programs do not activate Parquet. Do not mix system Arrow with PyArrow libraries or assume an unversioned -lparquet symlink exists. Extended data-file support Parquet options add projection, row-group selection, predicate pushdown, Hive datasets, checked temporal normalization, codecs, local atomic replacement/rewrite append, encrypted snapshot datasets, nullable write-schema evolution, fsync durability and cooperating-writer exclusion. Rich recursive schemas cross the existing opaque native handles and Arrow C Data boundary. CSVStream and ParquetStream name the incremental session APIs explicitly; use the module-level read_* / write_* functions for whole DataFrames. Dedicated file-format APIs and table interchange stdlib.csv owns CSV and stdlib.parquet owns Parquet. Their paired read_* / write_* functions operate on DataFrames; their unified session classes support explicit streaming. Shared Arrow/IPC classes stay here, with no format re-exports or DataFrame .to_* methods. See the CSV and Parquet guides. The matching irx.table_io Python helpers operate on pyarrow.Table through the native C Stream bridge, not Python CSV/Parquet engines. Whole-file reads drain validated batches into a chunked table, preserving empty schemas. Writes iterate TableBatchReader ; neither path uses CombineChunksToBatch() . Direct checked table casts validate every chunk and retain metadata/buffers. The older explicit conversion of a whole table to one RecordBatch may still combine chunks; it is not used by these convenience functions.
title: Native Apache Arrow Support

text: Architecture Arx collection syntax or IRx API -> ASTx collection nodes -> IRx semantic analysis and lowering -> IRx runtime feature activation -> generated LLVM calls irx_arrow_* / irx_rb_* symbols -> native Arrow C++ arrays, tensors, tables, and RecordBatches This boundary provides three useful properties: LLVM IR does not reproduce Arrow container layouts or ownership rules. Native runtime artifacts are compiled and linked only when a module needs them. Arrow C Data and Arrow IPC provide interoperable boundaries instead of a project-specific serialization format. Arx is Arrow-first, not Arrow-exclusive : supported scalar operations should prefer Arrow Scalar/compute where they implement Arx semantics, with LLVM/custom implementations for unsupported contracts. Control flow, classes, lists and files retain native language semantics. M0 does not yet change the existing scalar backend. The M0 architecture decision records representation, version, numerical and approval gates. The proposed imported scalar/Series stdlib.math.sqrt is not implemented by this baseline. IRx installs pyarrow and arx-arrowcpp-sources as runtime dependencies. They provide PyArrow interoperability plus the Arrow C++ headers, sources, library locations, and linker metadata used by native builds.
title: Native Apache Arrow Support · Architecture

text: Arx tensors and DataFrames Arx exposes the native runtime without exposing Arrow implementation types in the language syntax: fn first(grid: tensor[i32, 2, 2]) -> i32: return grid[0, 0] fn rows() -> i32: frame: dataframe[id: i32, score: f64] = dataframe({ id: [1, 2, 3], score: [0.5, 0.8, 1.0], }) scores: series[f64] = frame.score return cast(frame.nrows(), i32) Current tensor constraints: element types: i8 , i16 , i32 , i64 , f32 , and f64 variables, fields, and return types require a static shape tensor[T, ...] is supported for runtime-shaped parameters rank-one runtime-shaped parameters support checked numeric-sequence indexing; general runtime shape calculus and returns remain restricted Arrow-backed tensor storage is readonly in the current phase Current DataFrame constraints: static columns: numeric, Boolean, string and temporal types; nullable T | none constructor input: equal-length list-literal columns matching a static schema access: frame.name or frame["name"] when the schema is statically known metadata: nrows() and ncols() runtime-schema dataframe[...] locals, parameters and returns preserve RecordBatch-supported Arrow types/metadata through checked RecordBatch conversion; they do not provide unchecked static column access
title: Native Apache Arrow Support · Arx tensors and DataFrames

text: Array interoperability The lower-level IRx array runtime supports: signed and unsigned 8-, 16-, 32-, and 64-bit integers float32 , float64 , and Boolean arrays explicit array-builder and handle lifecycles Arrow C Data copy import, move/adopt import, and export null count and validity-bitmap inspection readonly irx_buffer_view projection for byte-addressable fixed-width arrays Boolean values are bit-packed in Arrow and therefore do not use the generic byte-addressable buffer-view bridge.
title: Native Apache Arrow Support · Array interoperability

text: RecordBatch IPC and PyArrow The Python API in irx.record_batch is backed by a standalone native Arrow C++ shared library. It supports: signed/unsigned integers, float32 , float64 , and bool utf8 and large_utf8 date32 , date64 second, millisecond, microsecond, and nanosecond timestamps time32 and time64 units nullable fields and null values Arrow IPC streams in files and in-memory buffers The test suite verifies both directions of interoperability: IRx-written IPC is read by PyArrow, and PyArrow-written IPC is read by IRx. The direct Python API builds a fingerprinted native shared library on first use. To pre-warm that cache explicitly: python -c "from irx.builder.runtime.record_batch import ensure_record_batch_shared_library; ensure_record_batch_shared_library()" Generated IRx programs use the runtime-feature system instead; their required native artifacts are collected during the normal build/link flow.
title: Native Apache Arrow Support · RecordBatch IPC and PyArrow

text: Deliberate boundaries Native Arrow support does not yet imply a complete Arrow product surface. The current implementation does not provide: an Arx query language or Arrow Compute kernel API dedicated RecordBatch syntax (use stdlib.arrow classes instead) general nested scalar access, dictionary, decimal, or arbitrary extension types mutable Tensor storage or a NumPy-compatible tensor algebra API automatic zero-copy guarantees for every import/export path These limits keep ownership, semantics, and compiler lowering explicit while the public APIs mature.
title: Native Apache Arrow Support · Deliberate boundaries

text: Compiled Arx interoperability ( stdlib.arrow ) stdlib.arrow exposes runtime-schema RecordBatches without changing the language grammar or converting them to statically typed DataFrames. It reuses the irx_rb_* implementation; the small irx_rb_api_* facade checks statuses before reading output slots and supplies scoped class-owned handles. The frontend only binds ASTx opaque types and native capabilities for the reserved bundled module. IRx performs normal class, call, FFI, ownership analysis and lowering. Importing unrelated standard-library modules does not activate the RecordBatch runtime.
title: Native Apache Arrow Support · Compiled Arx interoperability ( stdlib.arrow )

text: Build requirements and demonstrations Use the normal Arx development environment, including Clang, a C++20 compiler, PyArrow and arx-arrowcpp-sources . Native sources are compiled on demand through the existing runtime feature registry. The executable must be able to load the Arrow shared library used at link time; it does not start Python to serialize or deserialize data. The Python peer needs PyArrow; the demonstration runner also uses the compiler to build the Arx programs. From the repository root: python examples/arrow/run.py --directory .tmp/arrow-demo # Or choose --scenario files, --scenario c, or --scenario tcp. The runner uses temporary build/output paths chosen by --directory and ephemeral loopback ports . Its examples are also integration-test inputs: examples/arrow/write_file.x creates integer, floating-point and Boolean columns in compiled Arx and writes arx.arrow . Python uses pa.ipc.open_file and checks the schema and every value. examples/arrow/read_file.x reads python.arrow , created by Python with pa.ipc.new_file , and checks the full schema and every value. A separate test supplies a mismatched schema and requires failure. examples/arrow/tcp.x sends or receives two distinct RecordBatches . The runner builds real Arx launchers and exchanges standard IPC streaming bytes with a Python process over TCP in both directions. examples/arrow/types.x exercises every scalar append/get family, schema inspection, nullable values, empty batches, builder reuse and repeated close. examples/arrow/component.x builds a shared native component. Python invokes component__produce_stream / component__produce_array , then imports their outputs using PyArrow's _import_from_c APIs. The producing Arx locals have already been destroyed. The reverse functions consume PyArrow-exported data. This is compiled Arx, not the irx.record_batch Python wrapper.
title: Native Apache Arrow Support · Build requirements and demonstrations

text: Public API ``` title: Write a RecordBatch ``` import (Schema, BatchBuilder, RecordBatch, IPCWriter) from stdlib.arrow fn main() -> i32: schema: Schema = Schema() schema.add("id", "int64") schema.add("score", "float64") schema.add("active", "bool") builder: BatchBuilder = BatchBuilder(schema) builder.append_i64(0, 42) builder.append_f64(1, 1.5) builder.append_bool(2, true) batch: RecordBatch = builder.finish() writer: IPCWriter = IPCWriter(schema) writer.open_file("example.arrow") writer.write(batch) writer.close() return 0 Schema.add(name, type_name, nullable=false) accepts validated scalar names: Arrow scalar names Arx append/get suffix int8 , int16 , int32 , int64 i8 , i16 , i32 , i64 uint8 , uint16 , uint32 , uint64 Preserve/forward; no unsigned scalar getter float32 , float64 , bool f32 , f64 , bool utf8 , large_utf8 (also string , large_string ) utf8 date32[day] , date64[ms] date ( i64 count) timestamp[s] , timestamp[ms] , timestamp[us] , timestamp[ns] timestamp ( i64 count) time32[s] , time32[ms] , time64[us] , time64[ns] time ( i64 count) Numeric native IDs are not arguments to Schema.add ; complex schemas are imported from Arrow or read from Parquet. Types, units, timezones, nullability and metadata survive snapshots and IPC/C exports. Scalar builders/getters do not provide recursive construction or traversal. Class Operations Schema() add , nfields , name(col) , type(col) , type_name(col) , nullable(col) , equals(other) BatchBuilder(schema) append_<suffix>(col, value) , append_null(col) , finish() RecordBatch() Empty output holder; nrows , ncols , schema , is_null(col,row) , get_<suffix>(col,row) IPCReader() open_file(path) , open_stream(path) , connect(host,port,timeout_ms=30000) , next() , batch() , schema() IPCWriter(schema) open_file(path) , open_stream(path) , connect(host,port,timeout_ms=30000) , write(batch) All five classes have idempotent close() and automatic destruction at their last class reference. finish() resets the builder's column buffers for reuse; it does not destroy the builder. next() returns false only at end of stream, not for an empty batch. batch() returns an independent batch snapshot and is valid only after a successful next() . A reader's schema can be inspected before reading any batches. equals and write compare metadata as well as types and nullability. Close readers/writers before reopening them. Use open_file for the Arrow random-access file format , and open_stream for streaming format stored at a path . Both support multiple batches. Zero-field builders produce zero rows; imported zero-column batches retain their original row count. For nullable data, test is_null before a getter. Typed getters reject nulls and wrong types rather than inventing default values. Arx str cannot represent embedded NUL: getters reject such text explicitly; IPC and C sharing still preserve string values without conversion. Field names and timestamp timezone strings containing NUL can round-trip through IPC, but C schema export rejects them rather than silently truncating them. Arx operations use ARX-RUNTIME-ARROW-001 on failure and terminate the process, consistent with the current File API. No source location is invented for native failures (line/column are zero). Native embedding callers needing recoverable errors should use the status-returning irx_rb_* ABI, inspect irx_record_batch_errmsg() immediately, and never read output slots on error.
title: Native Apache Arrow Support · Public API

text: Same-process C Data and C Stream The native header irx_record_batch.h provides schema/batch export and move import, batch-to-stream export, and reader-to-stream export/import. It reuses irx_arrow_c_abi.h . Arrow C++ supplies the standard get_schema , get_next , get_last_error and release callbacks. No Arrow C++ layouts appear in LLVM. The pre-existing array C Data copy/move APIs remain available unchanged. Arx additionally provides: batch.export_c(array_address, schema_address) -> i32 batch.export_stream(stream_address) -> i32 batch.import_c(array_address, schema_address) reader.import_stream(stream_address) These addresses are trusted, same-process pointers encoded as i64 for the current 64-bit native targets. They are not serialized handles. Allocate zero-initialized standard structs in the host, keep their outer storage alive, and check export status before importing into PyArrow. Arbitrary addresses are unsafe. native_handle() is a borrowed opaque FFI escape hatch, not a transferable owner; never destroy it, wrap it in a second owning object, or use it after the class closes. Normal Arx code does not need this method. Exports retain Arrow buffers independently of the producing handle. Importing moves C ownership; after any attempted import, call a release callback only if it is still non-null. Import failures may already have consumed inputs. Native irx_rb_c_{array,schema,stream}_release helpers guard repeated release attempts on still-allocated outer structs , not on freed pointers. Raw opaque-handle release functions still free once and must not be called twice. irx_rb_stream_reader_export transfers the remaining iteration to the C stream; the original reader becomes exhausted and may be closed. Schema and array outputs outlive the stream. An array with release == NULL denotes end of stream; an empty batch has a live release callback. Stream callbacks are not thread-safe: serialize calls. Keep the producer shared library loaded until all exported objects have been released. RecordBatch C exports/imports share or adopt buffers without serialization; schema descriptors and wrapper objects allocate. IPC serializes data, socket reads allocate per-message buffers, and the existing buffer-input API copies its input. Existing array copy APIs also copy. These are not universal zero-copy guarantees . See the standard C Data and C Stream contracts.
title: Native Apache Arrow Support · Same-process C Data and C Stream

text: Across machines The Python peer listens and Arx connects, in either data direction. To move the loopback demonstration across hosts, run the Python listener on the receiving host (bind to its chosen interface), and compile the generated Arx launcher with that host's numeric IPv4 or IPv6 address and agreed port instead of loopback. Use send when Python reads with pa.ipc.open_stream(socket_file) , or receive when Python writes with pa.ipc.new_stream(socket_file, schema) . Close the Arrow writer before closing the socket so it emits the end marker. The runner's tcp() contains the complete Python peer and launcher implementation. Transport is separate from serialization ( irx_arrow_transport.* ). Native irx_rb_fd_reader_open / irx_rb_fd_writer_open duplicate a borrowed POSIX file descriptor, allowing host-supplied files/pipes as streaming endpoints. Closing these streams does not close the caller's descriptor; offsets are shared. For pipe writes, the host must arrange its SIGPIPE policy. TCP writes suppress SIGPIPE and handle partial writes, interrupted calls and connection failures. TCP is blocking, POSIX-only, numeric-address-only, with a positive connect and per-I/O timeout. It buffers messages/batches rather than an entire unbounded stream. This is not an untrusted network service : there is no authentication, TLS, batch-size quota, hostname resolution, listener API in Arx, or Flight. Use trusted peers and network controls. A slow peer can extend total transfer time by making progress; the timeout is not a whole-transfer deadline. Interop stream readers require an explicit Arrow end marker, even though some Arrow implementations accept transport EOF in its place. This detects a connection cut exactly between batches as well as truncated messages. Both PyArrow's normal writer close and the Arx writer emit this marker. A future Flight adapter can feed the same opaque batches/readers without changing the public data representation; Flight authentication and RPC are not part of this transport.
title: Native Apache Arrow Support · Across machines

text: Compatibility and limitations Capability Status Standalone Arx ↔ PyArrow IPC files and streams Implemented, multiple/empty batches Nullable numeric/Boolean, UTF-8 and temporal batches Runtime-schema API; checked typed methods Full field/schema metadata and timestamp timezone preservation IPC, C sharing and runtime-schema DataFrames; static casts use declared metadata Zero-column input with nonzero rows Preserved C Data/C Stream, both directions Standard structs; explicit ownership transfer TCP, both directions POSIX blocking clients; trusted numeric-address peers DataFrame ↔ RecordBatch conversion Checked exact scalar schemas, including nullable, unsigned, string and temporal columns Dictionary, decimal, binary and supported extensions Recursive C Data/IPC and Parquet forwarding; see format-specific limits Unsigned and supported nested values Forwarding supported; Arx scalar access/construction limited as above Arbitrary metadata editing, timestamp timezone creation in Arx Not exposed; imported schemas retain them Memory safety Functional ownership tests and a sanitizer harness; no blanket guarantee The sanitizer harness is packages/irx/tests/native/arrow_interop.cpp . Compile it with irx_record_batch.cpp , irx_arrow_transport.cc , irx_arrow_runtime.cc , the Arrow and buffer-native include/link flags, and -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer . It exercises schema snapshots, exported lifetimes, import moves, repeated guarded releases, EOF, CSV and checked table conversions, and corrupt-input cleanup. Pass a workspace-local CSV output path as its single argument. Arrow's prebuilt shared library itself is not sanitizer-instrumented by this command.
title: Native Apache Arrow Support · Compatibility and limitations

text: CSV streaming and checked conversion CSVStream in stdlib.csv and Python irx.record_batch reuses Arrow C++ streaming readers and writers. Python generic stream factories remain supported. Both cast(batch, dataframe[name:T, ...]) and cast(frame, RecordBatch) support exact static scalar schemas, including nullable columns. Literal-ellipsis dataframe[...] preserves runtime schemas with rich types and metadata. Conversion results own their references independently; DataFrame-to-RecordBatch export combines all chunks and may allocate. See CSV files and DataFrames for schemas, null rules, lifetime, streaming failure semantics and the intentionally restricted DataFrame subset.
title: Native Apache Arrow Support · CSV streaming and checked conversion

text: Explicit CSV and Parquet streams CSVStream and ParquetStream expose open_read , open_write , batch operations, schema and close , with one active session per owner. Parquet uses Arrow's native batch reader and buffered writer, not a whole-file Table or Python subprocess. The runtime owns the parent Parquet reader across C stream exports and checks footer finalization. Supported recursive types retain Arrow metadata; unsupported types and implicit temporal coercion are rejected. See Parquet files and DataFrames for the precise contract. The record_batch runtime links libarrow ; the dependent parquet feature adds the Parquet/Dataset/Compute/Acero libraries and format adapters. Use the registered feature artifacts and linker flags for native builds. The Python ctypes backend loads Parquet as a separate on-demand plugin. Arx analyzes all stdlib.arrow declarations but lowers only resolved reachable declarations; CSV-only programs do not activate Parquet. Do not mix system Arrow with PyArrow libraries or assume an unversioned -lparquet symlink exists.
title: Native Apache Arrow Support · Explicit CSV and Parquet streams

text: Extended data-file support Parquet options add projection, row-group selection, predicate pushdown, Hive datasets, checked temporal normalization, codecs, local atomic replacement/rewrite append, encrypted snapshot datasets, nullable write-schema evolution, fsync durability and cooperating-writer exclusion. Rich recursive schemas cross the existing opaque native handles and Arrow C Data boundary. CSVStream and ParquetStream name the incremental session APIs explicitly; use the module-level read_* / write_* functions for whole DataFrames.
title: Native Apache Arrow Support · Extended data-file support

text: Dedicated file-format APIs and table interchange stdlib.csv owns CSV and stdlib.parquet owns Parquet. Their paired read_* / write_* functions operate on DataFrames; their unified session classes support explicit streaming. Shared Arrow/IPC classes stay here, with no format re-exports or DataFrame .to_* methods. See the CSV and Parquet guides. The matching irx.table_io Python helpers operate on pyarrow.Table through the native C Stream bridge, not Python CSV/Parquet engines. Whole-file reads drain validated batches into a chunked table, preserving empty schemas. Writes iterate TableBatchReader ; neither path uses CombineChunksToBatch() . Direct checked table casts validate every chunk and retain metadata/buffers. The older explicit conversion of a whole table to one RecordBatch may still combine chunks; it is not used by these convenience functions.
title: Native Apache Arrow Support · Dedicated file-format APIs and table interchange

text: Built-in Types Choose explicit scalar types for arithmetic and annotated collection types for stored data. Accepted type spellings live in packages/arx/src/arx/lexer/syntax.json ; a lexical name alone does not establish executable support. See the capability matrix for that boundary and type annotations for placement. Scalars and conversions Use fixed-width integers or floats when width matters, bool for conditions, and str for UTF-8 text. char is a low-level i8 representation, not a Unicode grapheme. none is both the unit type and its sole value; a -> none function may use bare return , return none , or fall through. cast(value, Type) requests a supported conversion. isinstance(value, Type) checks the semantic type, including finite union aliases; type(value) returns its name. These do not introduce dynamic Python objects or runtime tagged unions. See the executable datatype tests and preview arithmetic contract . Strings have distinct static, borrowed, and owned lifetimes; consult the string ownership contract before returning or storing borrowed text. Native strings cannot represent embedded NUL safely. Parsing text fn distance(record: str) -> i64: clean: str = record.strip() return int(clean[1:]) For whitespace-delimited input, iterate over text.split() . The returned strings and list own their storage, including after the source file is closed or its text replaced. Advanced splitting can preserve empty fields with text.split(sep=",", maxsplit=2) ; strip(chars="xy") removes a set of code points, not the substring "xy" . Explicit empty separators fail. len(text) and indexing count Unicode code points, not bytes or grapheme clusters; no normalization occurs. Slices clip nonnegative bounds, but negative indices/bounds and non-unit steps are unsupported. ord(text) requires exactly one code point. int(text, base=10) returns checked i64 , with bases 2–36; unlike Python it does not recognize base prefixes or digit separators, and digits are ASCII only. Numeric casts still use cast , not int . Whitespace is locale-independent and shared by splitting, stripping and integer parsing; its exact set is specified in the native text source contract. Invalid text/options and overflow raise recoverable errors rather than returning partial data. Text literals and text-file reads reject embedded NUL; arbitrary octets use bytes and binary File methods instead. Byte values bytes([0, 255, 13, 10]) creates an immutable, length-aware octet buffer. bytes() is empty; bytes(existing) makes an independent copy. len(data) counts bytes and nonnegative indexing returns u8 ; indexing outside the buffer raises IndexError . NUL and invalid UTF-8 are ordinary bytes. This is not an Arrow binary column and does not require Arrow. Construction checks every integer in 0–255 without wrapping; Boolean, float, nullable, and text inputs are rejected. Sized integer sequences are accepted; single-pass iterators require an explicit max_items bound. An invalid value or exceeded bound publishes no partial buffer, but consumed input is not rewound. Unlike Python, scalar zero-fill construction, text encoding, and byte slices are not implemented. Content is immutable, but a local binding can be replaced. Buffers use the owned list lifecycle: parameters borrow; fresh results and returned local owners transfer ownership. Implicit local aliases are rejected: use bytes(existing) for a copy. Byte buffers in class/struct fields, nested containers, globals, extern signatures, and generator-owned storage are not supported. Independent binary reads can outlive their File. Collections and nullable values Collections and Apache Arrow owns the list, tensor, DataFrame, and Series storage rules. In particular, runtime-schema DataFrames support locals and returns, while runtime-shaped tensors remain parameter-only. Temporal and rich Arrow column schemas do not imply general temporal or nested scalar operations. Nullable expressions carry explicit validity, propagate nulls, and use checked arithmetic. They are not interchangeable with non-nullable scalar arithmetic or Boolean conditions. File references File and open create shared class references to one text or binary stream; lowercase file denotes the same type. References can be aliased, passed, returned, and stored in supported class fields. Closing through any alias closes the shared stream. Only the hidden native handle is uniquely owned.

text: Arx Capability Matrix This is the compact end-to-end support boundary, not a method catalog or a stability promise. Tokenization or an ASTx node alone does not establish Arx support. Package APIs and syntax may change before Arx 2.0 with coordinated caller updates and concise migration notes. Area Supported boundary Important limits Functions and types Name-first variables, parameter binding modifiers, initializer inference, named calls, bounded templates No parameter/return inference, first-class function values, closures, argument unpacking, or runtime tagged unions Numeric safety Lossless promotion, checked arithmetic/casts, scalar compound assignment, explicit wrapping 8–64-bit integers; no bigint fallback; typed recoverable dynamic failures Control flow if / elif / else , while , count loops, lazy-range/scalar-list for ... in , break / continue , try / except / else / finally , checked with No Arx general generators or context-exit suppression; see the exception boundary Modules and projects One entry graph; local, relative, namespace, stdlib and installed imports Cycles fail; no multiple direct CLI entries or executable module-level initialization Classes and files Acyclic shared identities, lifecycle hooks, string/File/class fields No owning list/Arrow fields, class containers, cycles, general foreign object ABI, or fatal cross-frame unwinding Lists and text Owned lists and Unicode text parsing; code-point indexing and clipped slices No negative text indices/bounds, non-unit text steps, embedded NUL, mutable list parameters, or owning generator captures Tensors Readonly fixed-shape numeric values; runtime-shaped parameters with checked rank-one indexing No general runtime shape calculus or runtime-shaped returns DataFrames and Series Static/rich schemas, runtime-schema locals/returns, exact checked casts, numeric/Boolean nullable expressions No unchecked runtime column access; rich storage does not imply rich scalar arithmetic CSV , Parquet , Arrow IPC Eager chunked frames, explicit streams, snapshots, C Data/C Stream interchange Native toolchain required; format restrictions apply; TCP is blocking/POSIX without TLS/Flight Native packages Declarative registered C ABI dependencies No raw-pointer source API, callbacks, plugins, or stable general FFI ABI CLI and tests Inspect, compile, run, and isolated compiled tests; structured diagnostics Host toolchain controls linking; no interactive shell Docstrings and lexical syntax Douki validation, UTF-8 source limits, Unicode locations Docstrings are omitted from AST/IR; then and operator declarations remain reserved; readonly/immutable/comptime modifiers are unsupported ArxPy provides Python parse/check/compile/run workflows. ArxJIT still executes Python fallback, not native dispatch. A support claim needs aligned frontend, ASTx, semantics, lowering/runtime, exports, and positive/negative tests. Unsupported input must fail at the earliest responsible boundary. Keep preview safety contracts and necessary workflow guidance synchronized; adding an API does not require another handwritten reference page.
title: Arx Capability Matrix

text: Classes Fields start with their names and accept inline declaration modifiers. Methods keep fn name(...) , with an optional group after -> : fn calculate(value: i32) -> public static :: i32: . The group modifies the method declaration, not the return type. Parameter var / const modifiers remain independent. Class Syntax class Counter(BaseCounter, Audited): version: public static const :: int32 = 1 value: int32 = 0 internal: private :: int32 = 1 fn get(self) -> int32: return self.value fn process(self, x: int32) -> protected :: int32: return x + 1 Optional class-level annotations use the same surface form: @[public, abstract] class Shape: fn area(self) -> public abstract :: float64 Template methods retain @<...> prefixes on their own lines before fn . Method modifiers move into the return tail: class Math: @<T: i32 | f64> fn identity(value: T) -> public static :: T: return value Modifier Rules Field modifiers are whitespace-separated in name: modifiers :: type ; method modifiers use fn name(...) -> modifiers :: type . Only classes retain comma-separated @[...] annotation lists. Method modifier annotations were removed rather than retained as a second spelling. Empty, duplicate, conflicting, floating, and invalid-target modifiers are rejected. Visibility is public , private , or protected . Fields support static and var / const ; methods retain static , abstract , and extern . Neither var nor const modifies a method name. Parameters use name: [var|const ::] type inside the existing method signature. The implicit self receiver is unchanged. Class const fields require declaration-site initialization, not deferred assignment in __init__ . override , virtual , final , sealed , readonly , and inline remain unsupported. See the declaration contract for binding stability, inference, and removed annotation spellings. Defaults Defaults are applied during parsing and normalization, not written back as implicit modifier groups. Fields default to public visibility and var binding policy. Methods default to public visibility. Only explicitly written modifiers are preserved as explicit metadata on the emitted IRx/ASTx nodes. For example, these declarations are equivalent semantically: value: int32 = 0 fn get(self) -> int32: return self.value value: public var :: int32 = 0 fn get(self) -> public :: int32: return self.value Construction And Typed Class Values Declared classes can be used in type annotations and construction expressions. Calls borrow objects; evaluated class arguments and receivers are pinned before later arguments can replace fields. The supported lifecycle names are __init__ and __del__ ; unknown names such as __inti__ or __str__ are semantic errors, including on static methods. Lifecycle hooks cannot be declared as fields. Dunders identify language-defined behavior, not private visibility or inheritance from a universal builtin superclass. Implementations are written by users; normal visibility annotations still apply. __init__(self, ...) -> none and __del__(self) -> none are compiler entry points, not ordinary callable methods. Explicit calls are rejected. Lifecycle hooks cannot be static, abstract, external, overloaded, templated, or variadic. Constructor defaults are existing scalar/string literals, not resource values. Shared ancestors initialize once in canonical base-first storage order. Each phase initializes its declared fields before calling its own __init__ . Final release reverses those phases, calling each __del__ before dropping its fields in reverse declaration order. This also works through a base-typed reference; non-prefix multiple-inheritance views locate concrete storage. Inside lifecycle hooks, self is only a field-access receiver: it cannot be aliased, returned, passed elsewhere, or used to invoke an ordinary self method. This prevents escape during construction and resurrection during destruction. These names are familiar from Python, but Arx keeps its own lifecycle contract: normal final-reference release synchronously runs cleanup, base phases chain automatically, and direct hook calls and resurrection are forbidden. An instance receiver is implicit; it cannot be supplied as a keyword. Keywords bind against the statically selected declaration, including through inheritance and dynamic dispatch. Generated calls propagate exceptions through those cleanup edges; an implicit destructor failure preserves an existing primary exception. Unrecoverable native failures do not promise cleanup. text: Collections and Apache Arrow Arx collection families have deliberately different semantics: Surface type Purpose Runtime representation range Immutable lazy integer progressions Inline fixed-size value list[T] General owned ordered values IRx dynamic-list runtime tensor[T, ...] Homogeneous N-dimensional numeric data Apache Arrow C++ arrow::Tensor dataframe[...] Heterogeneous named columns Apache Arrow C++ arrow::Table series[T] One typed DataFrame column Apache Arrow C++ arrow::ChunkedArray list is not an Arrow container. Tensor, DataFrame, and Series storage is provided by IRx's native Arrow C++ runtime. Lists fn sum_values() -> i32: values: list[i32] = [0, 1, 2 + 1] values.append(4) assert len(values) == 4 total: i32 = 0 for value in values: total = total + value return total Dynamic lists are move-only: owned locals and non-transferred temporaries are released on normal and exceptional lexical exits and replacement; returning an owned list moves it to the caller. A list moved into a pending return cannot be read or reassigned through that binding in finally ; a separate fresh owned return value is allowed. Parameters borrow storage and cannot append or return that borrow. Borrowed lists keep their exact element type: passing list[i32] to a list[i64] parameter does not convert the existing storage. While a for ... in loop borrows a list, replacing that owner binding anywhere in the body is a compile-time ownership error ( IRX-S013 ), including nested branches and exception clauses. Move the replacement after the loop or build a different list inside it; distinct shadowed bindings remain independent. Unlike Python, Arx does not retain the original list object across rebinding. In-place append remains allowed on owned locals, but iteration keeps its initial length, so appended elements are not visited. Returning the owner from the loop still moves it to the caller. Bracket expressions evaluate once, left to right, and produce owned lists; only an explicit fixed-shape tensor target selects tensor storage. An explicit list target types fresh literal elements first. Otherwise all elements must have a common lossless domain, independent of order. Empty lists need a target, for example values: list[i64] = [] . Nested owned lists remain unsupported. len(values) returns i64 ; narrowing it requires a checked cast . String insertion copies the bytes, and indexing or iterating a string list produces independent strings that survive list replacement. Failed construction drops initialized elements without replacing an existing destination. See the enforced list contract . Ranges are allocation-free values; see range workflows . Rank-one numeric tensors and typed Series also support len . Read-only numeric consumers sequence[T] is a parameter-only borrow , not a new owning container. Like Python's collections.abc.Sequence , it offers ordered iteration, integer indexing, and len -> i64 . Unlike Python sequences, negative indices, slicing, Boolean elements, and implicit element conversions are not supported. Numeric elements are signed/unsigned 8-64-bit integers or f32 / f64 . @<T: i32 | i64 | f64> fn first(values: sequence[T]) -> T: return values[0] Pass a matching list[T] , rank-one static/runtime tensor, or typed numeric Series directly. No flattening or conversion to f64 occurs; large integers remain exact. Nullable Series require sequence[nullable[T]] : explicitly fill or filter nulls for a nonnullable consumer. NaN and infinity remain floating values; algorithms needing finite input must check them. See the executable examples/numeric-sequences.x for inferred/explicit calls, nested template types, and nullable input. Ranges are not contiguous borrowed storage; materialize them explicitly with list(range(...), max_items=N) for these calls. Adapters live through the call or iteration, including exceptional exits. Lists borrow their owner; tensors pin their owner and preserve strides; Series retain independent zero-copy chunk snapshots so subsequent alias replacement does not invalidate the view. Sequence descriptors cannot be returned, stored, captured by a generator, reassigned, or used to mutate the source. Materialize an owned result instead: owned: list[i64] = list(values, max_items=1000) list(input, max_items=N) copies nonnullable numeric values once, including lazy ranges. Sized inputs may omit the bound; exceeding a supplied nonnegative bound raises ValueError without publishing a truncated list. Allocation sizes remain overflow-checked. Nullable storage is deliberately not supported in owned lists; fill/filter first. IRx single-pass generators are not sequences and require max_items . Materialization probes at most N + 1 items to detect excess, releasing partial output and owned temporary frames on failure. Consumption is not rolled back. Named frames remain owned by their lexical owner, but the acquired cursor is closed on success, early transfer, or failure. A second acquisition, including nested consumption, raises RuntimeError ; an acquisition failure caught inside an active loop does not close that loop's cursor. Arx source-level generator declarations are still unsupported; this iterator workflow is available to ASTx/IRx hosts, not new Arx yield syntax. Tensors Fixed-shape tensors use one or more integer dimensions: fn pick(grid: tensor[i32, 2, 2]) -> i32: return grid[1, 0] fn main() -> i32: grid: tensor[i32, 2, 2] = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] return pick(grid) Rules: supported elements: signed/unsigned 8-64-bit integers, f32 , and f64 literals must be rectangular and match the declared shape indexing supplies one index per static dimension variables, fields, and returns require at least one static dimension Tensor storage is readonly in the current implementation tensor[T, ...] accepts runtime shape/stride metadata at a function or extern parameter boundary: fn accept(values: tensor[i32, ...]) -> none: return none Indexing uses runtime rank, shape, strides, and offset. All indices must be nonnegative and in bounds, including dynamic indices into static-shaped tensors. Rank mismatch and invalid metadata fail before reading; byte-offset arithmetic is overflow-checked. Rank-one tensors also support len and ordered iteration. DataFrames and Series fn main() -> i32: rows: dataframe[id: i32, score: f64] = dataframe({ id: [1, 2, 3], score: [0.5, 0.8, 1.0], }) scores: series[f64] = rows.score ids: series[i32] = rows["id"] print(rows.ncols()) return cast(rows.nrows(), i32) Rules: columns support signed/unsigned numeric, Boolean and string values nullable columns use T | none ; date/time/timestamp columns can be populated through literal constructors or checked RecordBatch conversions the constructor accepts list-literal columns with equal row counts; it does not add implicit signed-to-unsigned coercion names and types must match the declared static schema statically known columns use rows.name or rows["name"] nrows() and ncols() return i64 dataframe[...] supports runtime-schema locals, parameters and returns, preserving rich Arrow types/metadata through RecordBatch casts; its columns cannot be accessed statically by name or silently narrowed Use read_csv / write_csv from stdlib.csv and read_parquet / write_parquet from stdlib.parquet for file I/O. Reads return independently owned runtime-schema frames; writes borrow frames and check finalization. No format-specific DataFrame methods or to_* aliases are added. CSVStream and ParquetStream in those modules support explicit streaming via frame() and write(frame) . Schema , BatchBuilder , RecordBatch and IPC remain in stdlib.arrow . File workflows and format-specific safety limits live in CSV and Parquet ; exact casts follow the shared conversion contract below. IPCReader.next() advances one batch; batch() and schema() return independent snapshots. open_file selects IPC file format, open_stream selects streaming format at a path, and connect exchanges IPC streaming bytes over TCP. Writers reject schema mismatches, including metadata and nullability. Check is_null before typed getters. Objects close on their last scoped reference; explicit close() is idempotent. See the interoperability workflow and ownership contract . Checked DataFrame conversion cast(frame, dataframe[id:i64]) and cast(batch, dataframe[id:i64]) assert exact names, order, physical types, and every chunk's reachable nullability. They do not project, coerce, fill nulls, or infer compile-time types. Metadata and independent ownership are preserved; cast(frame, RecordBatch) bridges back to batch APIs. Runtime-schema frames preserve rich Arrow data without permitting unchecked static column access. Fixed-row-count casts, owned globals, generator locals, aggregate-owned fields, and arbitrary DataFrame FFI are unsupported. See parameterized schemas for nested nullability and exact physical parameters. File-format restrictions still apply independently of what an in-memory frame can hold. Runtime boundary IRx activates native Arrow features only when lowering requires them. Generated LLVM calls opaque C ABI functions; Arrow C++ object layouts and ownership do not leak into LLVM structs or Arx syntax. See Native Apache Arrow Support for arrays, Arrow C Data, RecordBatch IPC, and current interoperability details. Nullable scalars and Series expressions nullable[T] stores a fixed-width numeric or Boolean scalar plus a validity bit. A nullable column is spelled series[T | none] . Indexing a nullable column returns nullable[T] ; indexing a non-nullable column returns T . Indices are zero-based; negative or out-of-range indices fail at runtime. ``` title: Nullable column expressions ``` fn main() -> i32: frame: dataframe[x:i32 | none] = dataframe({x:[1, none, 3]}) doubled: series[i32 | none] = frame.x + frame.x missing: nullable[i32] = doubled[1] assert is_null(missing) assert fill_null(doubled[2], 0) == 6 filled: series[i32] = fill_null(doubled, 7) assert filled[1] == 7 empty: nullable[i32] = none assert is_null(empty) return 0 Supported operators are + , - , * , / , == , != , < , <= , > and >= . Numeric operands use IRx common-type promotion. Column casts are checked; values that cannot be represented by the promoted type fail explicitly. Series/scalar operations broadcast the scalar. Series/Series operations require equal lengths. Integer arithmetic is checked: overflow and division by zero fail instead of wrapping. Null operands produce null outputs, including comparisons. Boolean && / and and || / or propagate nulls strictly, not with Kleene semantics. These operations are eager, not short-circuiting. is_null returns bool for a nullable scalar or a non-nullable Boolean Series mask. fill_null(value, replacement) eagerly evaluates a matching non-null scalar replacement and returns a non-nullable scalar or Series. Nullable scalars cannot implicitly become non-nullable values or conditions. Nullable scalar globals support numeric/Boolean literal or none initializers. Direct none is accepted in nullable declarations, assignments, returns, and function arguments/defaults. It never implicitly fills a non-nullable value. These scalar operations currently cover i8 – i64 , u8 – u64 , f32 , f64 and bool . String, temporal, decimal and nested Series retain their data and schema but cannot yet be indexed into language scalars or used in these operators. Unary + and checked - support signed numeric values; Boolean ! / not invert validity-preserving masks. Unsigned negation requires an explicit cast. Word not binds below comparisons, as in not frame.x == 3 ; see the Boolean evaluation contract . Remainder % is scalar-only and is rejected for nullable values and Series. column[start:stop:step] follows Python's bound clipping and negative-stride rules; omitted bounds are allowed and a zero step fails. Slicing, is_null and series_count also work on rich column storage. series_sum , series_min , series_max , series_mean , series_any and series_all skip nulls and return nullable scalars: empty/all-null input has a null result. series_count returns the non-null count as i64 . Integer sums use checked i64 / u64 accumulators; floating sums and means return f64 . Boolean reductions require Boolean columns. column[index] = value updates a mutable numeric/Boolean Series binding with bounds, type and nullability checks. Aliases of that handle observe updates; the originating DataFrame and previously computed/sliced Series do not. Construction completes before publication, so failed updates leave the old column intact. Concurrent access to a mutated handle is unsupported. Updates are statements, not value-producing assignment expressions. Returned Series own independent references; temporary columns and aliases are released by normal scope-lifetime cleanup. Parameterized static DataFrame schemas Checked RecordBatch casts additionally accept: decimal128[precision, scale] and decimal256[precision, scale] . timestamp["unit"] , timestamp["unit", "timezone"] , and time["unit"] , with units s , ms , us or ns . binary , binary[positive_size] , large_binary , and large_string . arrow_list[T] , large_list[T] , and fixed_list[T, positive_size] . dictionary[index_type, value_type] (unordered). arrow_map[key_type, value_type] and arrow_struct[name:T, ...] . For example, dataframe[amount:decimal128[12, 3] | none, items:arrow_list[nullable[i32]] | none] declares nullable decimal and list columns. Nested children are non-nullable unless wrapped in nullable[T] ; this wrapper models child nullability even for types that cannot be language scalars. Map keys cannot be nullable. Rich schemas work in aliases, parameters, returns and checked RecordBatch casts. Casts check names, order, exact physical parameters and nested nullability; non-nullable top-level columns also check actual batch null counts. They do not rescale decimals, change time units, or decode dictionaries implicitly. Input schema and field metadata are preserved. Unparameterized time uses time64 microseconds; timestamp / datetime use timezone-naive timestamp microseconds. Their text literal constructors accept whole seconds without timezone or fractional components. Use parameterized storage or checked Arrow imports for other units or zones. Rich DataFrame literals use the declared schema rather than inference. Decimal cells use exact strings or integers (not binary floats); binary cells use UTF-8 strings, with fixed widths checked in bytes. Parameterized temporal cells use integer storage units, without timezone conversion. Lists use nested lists; structs use positional lists matching declared field order; maps use lists of [key, value] pairs. Dictionaries encode literal values with checked index capacity. Nested nullability, widths, precision, scale and shape are validated during semantic analysis. Lowering embeds validated Arrow IPC bytes, not a Python interpreter or handwritten serialization format. Standalone rich scalar variables remain unsupported.
