text: Read-only numeric consumers sequence[T] is a parameter-only borrow , not a new owning container. Like Python's collections.abc.Sequence , it offers ordered iteration, integer indexing, and len -> i64 . Unlike Python sequences, negative indices, slicing, Boolean elements, and implicit element conversions are not supported. Numeric elements are signed/unsigned 8-64-bit integers or f32 / f64 . @<T: i32 | i64 | f64> fn first(values: sequence[T]) -> T: return values[0] Pass a matching list[T] , rank-one static/runtime tensor, or typed numeric Series directly. No flattening or conversion to f64 occurs; large integers remain exact. Nullable Series require sequence[nullable[T]] : explicitly fill or filter nulls for a nonnullable consumer. NaN and infinity remain floating values; algorithms needing finite input must check them. See the executable examples/numeric-sequences.x for inferred/explicit calls, nested template types, and nullable input. Ranges are not contiguous borrowed storage; materialize them explicitly with list(range(...), max_items=N) for these calls. Adapters live through the call or iteration, including exceptional exits. Lists borrow their owner; tensors pin their owner and preserve strides; Series retain independent zero-copy chunk snapshots so subsequent alias replacement does not invalidate the view. Sequence descriptors cannot be returned, stored, captured by a generator, reassigned, or used to mutate the source. Materialize an owned result instead: owned: list[i64] = list(values, max_items=1000) list(input, max_items=N) copies nonnullable numeric values once, including lazy ranges. Sized inputs may omit the bound; exceeding a supplied nonnegative bound raises ValueError without publishing a truncated list. Allocation sizes remain overflow-checked. Nullable storage is deliberately not supported in owned lists; fill/filter first. IRx single-pass generators are not sequences and require max_items . Materialization probes at most N + 1 items to detect excess, releasing partial output and owned temporary frames on failure. Consumption is not rolled back. Named frames remain owned by their lexical owner, but the acquired cursor is closed on success, early transfer, or failure. A second acquisition, including nested consumption, raises RuntimeError ; an acquisition failure caught inside an active loop does not close that loop's cursor. Arx source-level generator declarations are still unsupported; this iterator workflow is available to ASTx/IRx hosts, not new Arx yield syntax.
title: Collections and Apache Arrow · Read-only numeric consumers

text: Tensors Fixed-shape tensors use one or more integer dimensions: fn pick(grid: tensor[i32, 2, 2]) -> i32: return grid[1, 0] fn main() -> i32: grid: tensor[i32, 2, 2] = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] return pick(grid) Rules: supported elements: signed/unsigned 8-64-bit integers, f32 , and f64 literals must be rectangular and match the declared shape indexing supplies one index per static dimension variables, fields, and returns require at least one static dimension Tensor storage is readonly in the current implementation tensor[T, ...] accepts runtime shape/stride metadata at a function or extern parameter boundary: fn accept(values: tensor[i32, ...]) -> none: return none Indexing uses runtime rank, shape, strides, and offset. All indices must be nonnegative and in bounds, including dynamic indices into static-shaped tensors. Rank mismatch and invalid metadata fail before reading; byte-offset arithmetic is overflow-checked. Rank-one tensors also support len and ordered iteration.
title: Collections and Apache Arrow · Tensors

text: DataFrames and Series fn main() -> i32: rows: dataframe[id: i32, score: f64] = dataframe({ id: [1, 2, 3], score: [0.5, 0.8, 1.0], }) scores: series[f64] = rows.score ids: series[i32] = rows["id"] print(rows.ncols()) return cast(rows.nrows(), i32) Rules: columns support signed/unsigned numeric, Boolean and string values nullable columns use T | none ; date/time/timestamp columns can be populated through literal constructors or checked RecordBatch conversions the constructor accepts list-literal columns with equal row counts; it does not add implicit signed-to-unsigned coercion names and types must match the declared static schema statically known columns use rows.name or rows["name"] nrows() and ncols() return i64 dataframe[...] supports runtime-schema locals, parameters and returns, preserving rich Arrow types/metadata through RecordBatch casts; its columns cannot be accessed statically by name or silently narrowed Use read_csv / write_csv from stdlib.csv and read_parquet / write_parquet from stdlib.parquet for file I/O. Reads return independently owned runtime-schema frames; writes borrow frames and check finalization. No format-specific DataFrame methods or to_* aliases are added. CSVStream and ParquetStream in those modules support explicit streaming via frame() and write(frame) . Schema , BatchBuilder , RecordBatch and IPC remain in stdlib.arrow . File workflows and format-specific safety limits live in CSV and Parquet ; exact casts follow the shared conversion contract below. IPCReader.next() advances one batch; batch() and schema() return independent snapshots. open_file selects IPC file format, open_stream selects streaming format at a path, and connect exchanges IPC streaming bytes over TCP. Writers reject schema mismatches, including metadata and nullability. Check is_null before typed getters. Objects close on their last scoped reference; explicit close() is idempotent. See the interoperability workflow and ownership contract .
title: Collections and Apache Arrow · DataFrames and Series

text: Checked DataFrame conversion cast(frame, dataframe[id:i64]) and cast(batch, dataframe[id:i64]) assert exact names, order, physical types, and every chunk's reachable nullability. They do not project, coerce, fill nulls, or infer compile-time types. Metadata and independent ownership are preserved; cast(frame, RecordBatch) bridges back to batch APIs. Runtime-schema frames preserve rich Arrow data without permitting unchecked static column access. Fixed-row-count casts, owned globals, generator locals, aggregate-owned fields, and arbitrary DataFrame FFI are unsupported. See parameterized schemas for nested nullability and exact physical parameters. File-format restrictions still apply independently of what an in-memory frame can hold.
title: Collections and Apache Arrow · Checked DataFrame conversion

text: Runtime boundary IRx activates native Arrow features only when lowering requires them. Generated LLVM calls opaque C ABI functions; Arrow C++ object layouts and ownership do not leak into LLVM structs or Arx syntax. See Native Apache Arrow Support for arrays, Arrow C Data, RecordBatch IPC, and current interoperability details.
title: Collections and Apache Arrow · Runtime boundary

text: Nullable scalars and Series expressions nullable[T] stores a fixed-width numeric or Boolean scalar plus a validity bit. A nullable column is spelled series[T | none] . Indexing a nullable column returns nullable[T] ; indexing a non-nullable column returns T . Indices are zero-based; negative or out-of-range indices fail at runtime. ``` title: Nullable column expressions ``` fn main() -> i32: frame: dataframe[x:i32 | none] = dataframe({x:[1, none, 3]}) doubled: series[i32 | none] = frame.x + frame.x missing: nullable[i32] = doubled[1] assert is_null(missing) assert fill_null(doubled[2], 0) == 6 filled: series[i32] = fill_null(doubled, 7) assert filled[1] == 7 empty: nullable[i32] = none assert is_null(empty) return 0 Supported operators are + , - , * , / , == , != , < , <= , > and >= . Numeric operands use IRx common-type promotion. Column casts are checked; values that cannot be represented by the promoted type fail explicitly. Series/scalar operations broadcast the scalar. Series/Series operations require equal lengths. Integer arithmetic is checked: overflow and division by zero fail instead of wrapping. Null operands produce null outputs, including comparisons. Boolean && / and and || / or propagate nulls strictly, not with Kleene semantics. These operations are eager, not short-circuiting. is_null returns bool for a nullable scalar or a non-nullable Boolean Series mask. fill_null(value, replacement) eagerly evaluates a matching non-null scalar replacement and returns a non-nullable scalar or Series. Nullable scalars cannot implicitly become non-nullable values or conditions. Nullable scalar globals support numeric/Boolean literal or none initializers. Direct none is accepted in nullable declarations, assignments, returns, and function arguments/defaults. It never implicitly fills a non-nullable value. These scalar operations currently cover i8 – i64 , u8 – u64 , f32 , f64 and bool . String, temporal, decimal and nested Series retain their data and schema but cannot yet be indexed into language scalars or used in these operators. Unary + and checked - support signed numeric values; Boolean ! / not invert validity-preserving masks. Unsigned negation requires an explicit cast. Word not binds below comparisons, as in not frame.x == 3 ; see the Boolean evaluation contract . Remainder % is scalar-only and is rejected for nullable values and Series. column[start:stop:step] follows Python's bound clipping and negative-stride rules; omitted bounds are allowed and a zero step fails. Slicing, is_null and series_count also work on rich column storage. series_sum , series_min , series_max , series_mean , series_any and series_all skip nulls and return nullable scalars: empty/all-null input has a null result. series_count returns the non-null count as i64 . Integer sums use checked i64 / u64 accumulators; floating sums and means return f64 . Boolean reductions require Boolean columns. column[index] = value updates a mutable numeric/Boolean Series binding with bounds, type and nullability checks. Aliases of that handle observe updates; the originating DataFrame and previously computed/sliced Series do not. Construction completes before publication, so failed updates leave the old column intact. Concurrent access to a mutated handle is unsupported. Updates are statements, not value-producing assignment expressions. Returned Series own independent references; temporary columns and aliases are released by normal scope-lifetime cleanup.
title: Collections and Apache Arrow · Nullable scalars and Series expressions

text: Parameterized static DataFrame schemas Checked RecordBatch casts additionally accept: decimal128[precision, scale] and decimal256[precision, scale] . timestamp["unit"] , timestamp["unit", "timezone"] , and time["unit"] , with units s , ms , us or ns . binary , binary[positive_size] , large_binary , and large_string . arrow_list[T] , large_list[T] , and fixed_list[T, positive_size] . dictionary[index_type, value_type] (unordered). arrow_map[key_type, value_type] and arrow_struct[name:T, ...] . For example, dataframe[amount:decimal128[12, 3] | none, items:arrow_list[nullable[i32]] | none] declares nullable decimal and list columns. Nested children are non-nullable unless wrapped in nullable[T] ; this wrapper models child nullability even for types that cannot be language scalars. Map keys cannot be nullable. Rich schemas work in aliases, parameters, returns and checked RecordBatch casts. Casts check names, order, exact physical parameters and nested nullability; non-nullable top-level columns also check actual batch null counts. They do not rescale decimals, change time units, or decode dictionaries implicitly. Input schema and field metadata are preserved. Unparameterized time uses time64 microseconds; timestamp / datetime use timezone-naive timestamp microseconds. Their text literal constructors accept whole seconds without timezone or fractional components. Use parameterized storage or checked Arrow imports for other units or zones. Rich DataFrame literals use the declared schema rather than inference. Decimal cells use exact strings or integers (not binary floats); binary cells use UTF-8 strings, with fixed widths checked in bytes. Parameterized temporal cells use integer storage units, without timezone conversion. Lists use nested lists; structs use positional lists matching declared field order; maps use lists of [key, value] pairs. Dictionaries encode literal values with checked index capacity. Nested nullability, widths, precision, scale and shape are validated during semantic analysis. Lowering embeds validated Arrow IPC bytes, not a Python interpreter or handwritten serialization format. Standalone rich scalar variables remain unsupported.
title: Collections and Apache Arrow · Parameterized static DataFrame schemas

text: Arx Compiler CLI The arxlang distribution installs the arx command. It can inspect frontend and lowering stages, compile native artifacts, run executables, and execute compiled tests. Command forms arx [input_file] [options] arx run [input_file] [options] arx test [paths ...] [options] run is an alternate spelling of --run . test is a separate subcommand. Inspection modes arx --show-tokens program.x arx --show-ast program.x arx --show-llvm-ir program.x These modes stop after printing the requested representation. Build and run arx program.x --output-file program arx --run program.x arx run program.x The compiler emits an executable when the module defines main . Without a native entry point, or with --lib , it emits an object artifact instead. Use arx --help for the complete option list and defaults rather than a copied flag catalog. Diagnostics and linker choices below have operational consequences. Compiling multiple input files in one invocation is not currently supported. Use project-aware imports to compile a module graph from one entry file. Output path --output-file accepts the requested artifact path. If it is omitted, the compiler derives a name from the entry source file and otherwise falls back to a.out . Link modes The default auto mode uses the platform toolchain's default executable mode. pie and no-pie request explicit position-independent or non-PIE linking. If a linker defaults to PIE but rejects an object relocation, use: arx program.x --link-mode no-pie IRx emits PIC-compatible objects by default. Explicit link modes are primarily toolchain compatibility controls. Diagnostics Expected lexer, parser, semantic, lowering, native compilation, and linking failures exit with status 1. Human-readable diagnostics go to standard error by default. Unexpected internal failures produce ARX-INTERNAL-001 without exposing exception details and exit with status 70. Compiler developers can opt in to the original Python exception and traceback with --traceback . Use --diagnostic-format json for one versioned JSON document on standard error: { "diagnostics": [ { "code": "ARX-PARSE-001", "column": 7, "end_column": null, "end_line": null, "hint": null, "line": 4, "message": "expected expression", "module": null, "notes": [], "phase": "frontend", "severity": "error" } ], "schema_version": 1 } JSON mode covers expected compiler-phase failures and sanitized internal failures. Argument usage errors remain argparse text with exit status 2. Consumers must reject unsupported schema_version values instead of guessing field semantics. Exit status Meaning 0 command succeeded 1 expected compiler/source failure 2 CLI usage or input-path failure 70 unexpected internal compiler failure Tests The arx test subcommand has its own discovery and execution options. See Compiled Tests . API boundary CLI argument handling lives in Arx. Semantic diagnostics, LLVM lowering, artifact building, and runtime feature activation are provided by IRx.
title: Arx Compiler CLI

text: Control Flow Arx supports if / elif / else , while , and two for loop styles. Declaration Scopes Each if , elif , or else arm and each loop body has a lexical declaration scope. A declaration is visible only in its enclosing scope and nested bodies; it cannot be read after that scope ends, even if that body always executes. Sibling bodies may reuse a name, and inner declarations may shadow outer ones. Assignment without a declaration updates the nearest visible binding instead. This differs from Python's function-wide local declarations. Declaring the same name twice in one scope is an error. Function parameters and the top-level function body share a scope; a loop target and its body also share their loop scope. Leaving a body releases its local owners on fallthrough or control transfer, without releasing shadowed outer owners. See the ownership contract for resource-specific rules. If / Elif / Else Conditions must be Boolean and are evaluated in order, stopping at the first match. A chain may have any number of elif clauses and an optional final else . Align every clause with its opening if ; use elif , not else if . ``` title: Conditional chain example summary: Classifies an integer using ordered comparisons. ``` fn classify(value: i32) -> i32: ``` title: classify summary: Classifies one integer as negative, zero, or positive. ``` if value < 0: return 0 - 1 elif value == 0: return 0 else: return 1 While Loop ``` title: While loop example summary: Repeats while condition is true. ``` fn count_to_ten() -> i32: ``` title: count_to_ten summary: Increments value until it reaches ten. ``` a: i32 = 0 while a < 10: a = a + 1 return a For Loop (For-In Style) For-in loops iterate over ranges and supported sequences, including list literals and list variables: for i in <iterable-expression>: ``` title: Range-style for loop summary: Iterates from start to end with the builtin range helper. ``` fn range_loop(n: i32) -> i32: ``` title: range_loop summary: Sums values produced by a range loop. ``` total: i32 = 0 for i in range(0, n): total = total + i return total range(stop) and range(start, stop[, step]) produce immutable range values, not lists. Named start , stop , and step are supported. Endpoints and elements are i32 ; internal arithmetic and len use i64 . Storage is constant-size, and each iteration has an independent cursor. Rebinding the input does not replace an active cursor's snapshot. Integer indexing is checked; negative indices and slicing are unsupported. Zero step raises AssertionError , even for an empty interval. Request list storage explicitly with list(values, max_items=N) ; exceeding the bound raises ValueError without publishing a truncated prefix. There is no implicit allocation when passing a range to a list or numeric-sequence consumer. You can also iterate over a list literal or a list variable: ``` title: List for-in loop summary: Iterates over one list variable and one list literal. ``` fn list_loop() -> i32: ``` title: list_loop summary: Sums values from two list-valued loop inputs. ``` values: list[i32] = list(range(3)) total: i32 = 0 for value in values: total = total + value for value in [3, 4]: total = total + value return total The old colon range header syntax was removed. Use builtin range(...) or any other supported iterable expression instead. For Loop (Count Style) Count-style loops follow: for i: type = init; condition; update: ``` title: Count-style for loop summary: Uses initializer, condition, and update expressions. ``` fn count_loop() -> i32: ``` title: count_loop summary: Sums numbers from 0 to 4. ``` total: i32 = 0 for i: i32 = 0; i < 5; i += 1: total += i return total Compound updates write the induction variable themselves. Ordinary expression updates such as i + 1 remain supported; the loop stores their result into i . See the compound assignment contract . Break and Continue break exits the nearest enclosing loop. continue starts its next iteration; in a count loop it runs the update first. Both are operand-free statements and are rejected outside loops. They work in while , count, and supported for-in loops, including nested loops. ``` title: Skip values and stop early ``` fn main() -> i32: total: i32 = 0 for value in range(1000000): if value == 0: continue if value == 4: break total += value assert total == 6 return 0 Loop transfers release exited-scope owners and run finally before advancing or leaving the loop. A cleanup failure cancels the transfer and propagates as an exception; an explicit finalizer can replace it with another transfer, return, or exception. Active iteration borrows end when their loop is exited. Return Statements return expr returns a value from the current function. Inside none -returning functions, use a bare return , return none , or omit the return statement entirely. Indentation Rules Blocks start after : . The next logical line must be indented by one level (2 spaces in Arx style). Misaligned indentation is treated as a parser error.
title: Control Flow

text: CSV files and DataFrames Import CSV operations from stdlib.csv . Shared Arrow schemas, batches and IPC remain in stdlib.arrow ; CSV is backed by Arrow C++, not a Python process or a second parser. The native Arrow libraries and a C++ toolchain are required. Read and write a DataFrame ``` title: Copy a CSV file ``` import (read_csv, write_csv) from stdlib.csv fn main() -> i32: ``` title: Read every row and finalize the output ``` frame: dataframe[...] = read_csv("input.csv") write_csv(frame, "output.csv") return 0 These eager functions close their internal session before returning. Reads return an independent, chunked DataFrame; writes borrow the frame without consuming or mutating it. Temporary inputs such as write_csv(read_csv("input.csv"), "output.csv") are supported. The result must fit in memory: block_size controls parsing blocks, not total memory. Writers return none only after checked finalization. There are no DataFrame .to_* methods or to_* aliases. Never copy a file onto itself using streaming sessions. Parsing policy An omitted schema is inferred from the first block, then frozen. For headerless input, supply a schema or explicit names; names requires header=false and no schema. Projections must be nonempty and unique and preserve requested order. null_values replaces token recognition; an empty list disables it. These choices affect interpretation, not just performance. The eager option schema lives in irx.analysis.table_io ; defaults and validation are implemented by the native CSV options code. Python signatures are in the generated table_io reference. Stream declarations and contracts live in packages/arx/src/arx/stdlib/csv.x . Arx name/column/token arguments are literal lists, not arbitrary iterable objects. Unknown options and unsupported types fail explicitly. Delimiter, quote and escape bytes must not conflict; NUL, CR and LF are not valid dialect characters. Output quoting uses Arrow's fixed double-quote convention; this is not a complete Python csv dialect engine. CSV projection happens after full input validation and conversion . A bad unselected field still fails. Explicit schemas check header names/order/count and nullability; they control parsing rather than merely asserting types. Checked DataFrame conversion import Schema from stdlib.arrow import read_csv from stdlib.csv # Inside a function: schema: Schema = Schema() schema.add("id", "int64", nullable=false) loaded: dataframe[...] = read_csv("ids.csv", schema=schema) ids: dataframe[id:i64] = cast(loaded, dataframe[id:i64]) Runtime schemas do not infer compile-time column types. The cast above asserts an exact schema; it does not project or coerce data. See the shared checked DataFrame conversion contract for nullability, chunk validation, metadata, and ownership restrictions. CSV supports integer widths, floating point, Boolean, UTF-8/large UTF-8, dates, timestamps and time units. Nested/other unsupported types fail; use Parquet or IPC for those. CSV does not encode type/schema metadata. Supply an explicit schema to preserve widths and temporal units on a roundtrip. Explicit streaming Use CSVStream for incremental processing instead of loading the entire file into a DataFrame. It supports either read or write mode. import CSVStream from stdlib.csv # Inside a function: source: CSVStream = CSVStream() source.open_read("large.csv") while source.next(): chunk: dataframe[...] = source.frame() print(chunk.nrows()) source.close() CSVStream() starts closed and has one read or write mode. open_read_as(path, schema, ...) supplies an explicit schema; open_write(path, schema, ...) configures output. These session factories expose delimiter/header and read block size. The additional dialect controls above belong to the eager functions. next() advances; false means EOF, not an empty batch. frame() snapshots the current batch without advancing and survives reader closure. It fails before a successful next() or after EOF. write(frame) and write(batch) require an exact schema. batch() and schema() remain available for Arrow interoperability. Call writer close() explicitly to observe finalization errors; automatic cleanup alone is not proof of success. Wrong-mode access fails, aliases share session state, and failed sessions cannot be reused. The streaming roundtrip example processes every batch. The table example converts CSV to Parquet using only the module-level functions. Text and failure contract UTF-8 and quoted multiline fields are supported. By default only unquoted empty fields are null. Quoted "" remains an empty string; NA and NULL remain text unless configured in null_values . Custom na_rep requires matching read null_values . Non-null unquoted data equal to a null marker is ambiguous; a lossless roundtrip is not guaranteed. Blank one-column rows remain null rows unless explicitly skipped. Malformed record widths fail; skiprows does not enable malformed-row skipping. Headers must be nonempty and unique. Typed header-only input succeeds; completely empty files fail. Inferred null/binary columns need an explicit supported schema or corrected input. CSV has no remote URLs, compression/encoding discovery, append or atomic writes. Validation precedes truncation, but later data/I/O failures can leave partial output. A failed eager read never returns a partial table. Compiled failures use ARX-RUNTIME-ARROW-001 , with typed catchable Arx exceptions. CSV row positions are not invented as Arx source locations. Python integration from irx.table_io import read_csv, write_csv frame = read_csv("input.tsv", delimiter="\t", columns=["id", "name"]) write_csv(frame, "output.csv") These functions return/accept pyarrow.Table , accept string or PathLike paths, and use IRx native sessions/C Stream interchange, not Python format engines. Use pyarrow.Schema for schema . Selectors accept checked sequences. Imports do not compile native code; CSV-only use does not load Parquet, Dataset or Acero. Stale native-library overrides produce a rebuild/unset error. For streaming, irx.record_batch.CSVStream and the lower-level RecordBatchStreamReader.open_csv / RecordBatchStreamWriter.open_csv remain available. Iteration releases its batch on advancement; batch.to_arrow() exports independent Arrow references. Release manually retained batch/schema snapshots explicitly.

text: Read and write a DataFrame ``` title: Copy a CSV file ``` import (read_csv, write_csv) from stdlib.csv fn main() -> i32: ``` title: Read every row and finalize the output ``` frame: dataframe[...] = read_csv("input.csv") write_csv(frame, "output.csv") return 0 These eager functions close their internal session before returning. Reads return an independent, chunked DataFrame; writes borrow the frame without consuming or mutating it. Temporary inputs such as write_csv(read_csv("input.csv"), "output.csv") are supported. The result must fit in memory: block_size controls parsing blocks, not total memory. Writers return none only after checked finalization. There are no DataFrame .to_* methods or to_* aliases. Never copy a file onto itself using streaming sessions.
title: CSV files and DataFrames · Read and write a DataFrame

text: Parsing policy An omitted schema is inferred from the first block, then frozen. For headerless input, supply a schema or explicit names; names requires header=false and no schema. Projections must be nonempty and unique and preserve requested order. null_values replaces token recognition; an empty list disables it. These choices affect interpretation, not just performance. The eager option schema lives in irx.analysis.table_io ; defaults and validation are implemented by the native CSV options code. Python signatures are in the generated table_io reference. Stream declarations and contracts live in packages/arx/src/arx/stdlib/csv.x . Arx name/column/token arguments are literal lists, not arbitrary iterable objects. Unknown options and unsupported types fail explicitly. Delimiter, quote and escape bytes must not conflict; NUL, CR and LF are not valid dialect characters. Output quoting uses Arrow's fixed double-quote convention; this is not a complete Python csv dialect engine. CSV projection happens after full input validation and conversion . A bad unselected field still fails. Explicit schemas check header names/order/count and nullability; they control parsing rather than merely asserting types.
title: CSV files and DataFrames · Parsing policy

text: Checked DataFrame conversion import Schema from stdlib.arrow import read_csv from stdlib.csv # Inside a function: schema: Schema = Schema() schema.add("id", "int64", nullable=false) loaded: dataframe[...] = read_csv("ids.csv", schema=schema) ids: dataframe[id:i64] = cast(loaded, dataframe[id:i64]) Runtime schemas do not infer compile-time column types. The cast above asserts an exact schema; it does not project or coerce data. See the shared checked DataFrame conversion contract for nullability, chunk validation, metadata, and ownership restrictions. CSV supports integer widths, floating point, Boolean, UTF-8/large UTF-8, dates, timestamps and time units. Nested/other unsupported types fail; use Parquet or IPC for those. CSV does not encode type/schema metadata. Supply an explicit schema to preserve widths and temporal units on a roundtrip.
title: CSV files and DataFrames · Checked DataFrame conversion

text: Explicit streaming Use CSVStream for incremental processing instead of loading the entire file into a DataFrame. It supports either read or write mode. import CSVStream from stdlib.csv # Inside a function: source: CSVStream = CSVStream() source.open_read("large.csv") while source.next(): chunk: dataframe[...] = source.frame() print(chunk.nrows()) source.close() CSVStream() starts closed and has one read or write mode. open_read_as(path, schema, ...) supplies an explicit schema; open_write(path, schema, ...) configures output. These session factories expose delimiter/header and read block size. The additional dialect controls above belong to the eager functions. next() advances; false means EOF, not an empty batch. frame() snapshots the current batch without advancing and survives reader closure. It fails before a successful next() or after EOF. write(frame) and write(batch) require an exact schema. batch() and schema() remain available for Arrow interoperability. Call writer close() explicitly to observe finalization errors; automatic cleanup alone is not proof of success. Wrong-mode access fails, aliases share session state, and failed sessions cannot be reused. The streaming roundtrip example processes every batch. The table example converts CSV to Parquet using only the module-level functions.

text: Data Types Arx is statically typed. Function parameters and return types use explicit annotations. Variables may select a type explicitly or request initializer-based inference with auto . Type Annotations Function parameters must always be typed. Function return type is declared with -> type and is always required, including -> none . An explicit annotation selects a type: count: i32 = 1 . count: auto = 1 infers a concrete, fixed type from its required initializer. auto is an inference marker, not a dynamic type, and is not allowed in function signatures. See declarations for supported inference contexts. Binding mutability is independent of the selected or inferred type: count: var :: i32 = 1 permits rebinding; limit: const :: auto = 10 does not. Omitting the modifier means var ; const does not freeze referenced objects. auto remains contextual for value identifiers, but cannot name a class, type alias, or template parameter. ``` title: Typed function signature summary: Demonstrates required parameter annotations. ``` fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32: ``` title: add summary: Returns a + b. ``` return a + b Collection annotations Runtime-shaped tensor[T, ...] remains parameter-only; indexed access requires a fixed shape. Runtime-schema dataframe[...] supports locals, aliases, parameters, and returns, but not unchecked named-column access. These are different restrictions. See collections for storage, construction, exact schema casts, and nullable operations. Type Aliases And Union Types Type aliases are top-level declarations. The type word is contextual, so type Name = ... declares an alias while type(value) calls the builtin type-name helper. ``` title: Type alias example summary: Demonstrates a finite numeric union alias. ``` type Number = i32 | i64 fn identity(value: Number) -> Number: ``` title: identity summary: Returns a numeric union value. ``` return value Union annotations use | . Numeric unions currently lower through a shared lossless numeric storage type; incompatible runtime unions are rejected. Generic union bounds constrain template membership without allocating union storage. Runtime tagged unions and runtime narrowing are not part of the current model. Choosing a type See Built-in Types for scalar choices and conversion boundaries. The lexical manifest owns accepted spellings; it is not an API support promise. Class References Declared class names denote identity-preserving, reference-managed object pointers. Local copies and owned returns keep objects alive; final release runs __del__ and drops owned fields. Acyclic instance class/string/file fields are supported, but class values in containers/unions/structs, globals/statics, and generators are rejected. See Classes for construction and lifetime rules; there is no general external ownership ABI.

text: Docstrings Arx docstrings use the Douki YAML format and are validated against the official Douki schema . Docstrings are delimited by triple backticks: ``` title: Example docstring summary: Optional summary value. ``` Supported Targets (Current) module docstring class docstring function docstring method docstring Required Field Every docstring must provide at least: title (required by Douki schema) Valid minimal docstring: ``` title: Add two numbers ``` Module Docstring Rule The module docstring must: be the first top-level statement start at line 1, column 1 (no leading spaces) Valid: ``` title: Module docs ``` fn main() -> i32: ``` title: main summary: Entry point for the module. ``` return 1 Function Docstring Rule A function docstring, when present, must be the first statement in the function body, right after : and the required newline/indentation. The parser does not require a docstring in every user function; repository source-contract conventions still apply. Valid: fn main() -> i32: ``` title: Function docs summary: Function summary ``` return 1 Invalid: fn main() -> i32: return 1 ``` title: Too late summary: This docstring is valid Douki but in the wrong position. ``` Class and method docstrings A class docstring may appear as the first item in an indented class body, before fields or methods. Method docstrings follow the same first-body-item rule as function docstrings. Abstract methods can use a docstring-only body so the docstring still belongs to the method block. Current Compiler Behavior Docstrings are currently lexed and validated for: placement rules (module, class, function, and method positions) Douki YAML schema conformance After validation, they are intentionally ignored during AST/IR generation until dedicated DocString nodes are added in astx and irx .

text: File I/O File is a builtin reference-managed class for a deliberately small native, POSIX text and binary file interface. open(...) is a compiler-backed factory adapter to File(...) : both create the same class object through one checked construction path. Both are available without an import and use C stdio, not Python or Arrow. Lowercase file remains a compatibility spelling for the builtin File type. The default is a strict UTF-8 text read. Use mode="w" to create/truncate or mode="a" to append. Only the path and mode can be runtime strings; other Python-shaped settings accept only the implemented default profile. Nondefault buffering, encodings, error policies, newline handling, descriptors, and openers are rejected rather than ignored. Options are checked before I/O; a dynamic mode is checked before opening or truncating a path. Paths are relative to the running program's working directory, not its source file. Reading requires an existing file. Writing creates or truncates it. Appending creates it if necessary and writes at the end. Update/exclusive modes, file descriptors, callbacks, and custom buffering are unsupported. Binary modes are rb , wb , and ab ; non- none encoding, errors, or newline options are rejected before creating/truncating a path, including when the mode is dynamic. Example Run this in a scratch directory: the example creates/truncates message.txt . ``` title: Native text file example ``` fn main() -> i32: ``` title: main ``` with open("message.txt", mode="w", encoding="utf-8") as output: assert output.write("hello\n") == 6 with open(file="message.txt") as source: print(source.read()) return 0 Checked resource scopes Inside a function, with manager [as name]: evaluates one manager once. A successful __enter__ is followed by exactly one __exit__ on fallthrough, return, loop transfer, or failure. Failed acquisition does not call exit. The optional name is scoped to the body and cannot be rebound; it does not freeze the referenced object. Multiple managers and destructuring targets are unsupported; nest scopes instead. File entry returns the same reference and rejects an already-closed stream without reading, writing, or flushing it. Exit performs checked close, including buffered write errors; all retained aliases then refer to a closed stream. Rebinding the original manager does not change which object gets closed. Explicit close inside the body is safe because close is idempotent. If both the body and implicit exit fail, the body error stays primary and the exit error is retained as a secondary diagnostic. An exit-only failure is catchable. Exit cannot suppress errors, unlike Python's protocol, and does not have explicit finally 's completion-replacement behavior. Closure is not rollback, atomic publication, or durability: writes may already be visible. Bounded binary workflow Use bytes([0, 255, 13, 10]) for octets, then output.write_bytes(data) on a binary stream. source.read_bytes(size) reads at most a nonnegative i64 byte count; there is no read-all sentinel. It returns independently owned bytes , including empty at EOF. Zero does not advance but still checks mode and closed state. Text methods reject binary streams and byte methods reject text streams. Nothing decodes, strips NUL, or translates newlines. examples/binary-files.x is an executable round-trip and append example. It creates/truncates binary-output.dat and binary-empty.dat ; run it in a scratch directory. Byte lengths and write counts are bytes, not characters. Short writes that make progress are retried; no progress and I/O errors are failures. Failure may leave a partially modified external file: there is no rollback, atomicity, or durability promise. Checked scope exit or explicit flush/close still matter for buffered errors. See byte values for immutable-buffer ownership. Text and lifetime safety Reads consume all remaining text (not a size-limited chunk), returning an independent string or "" at EOF. CRLF and CR become LF; malformed UTF-8 and embedded NUL fail. Write counts are Unicode characters, not bytes. Explicit flush checks buffered writes without promising durability. Close is idempotent; other operations on a closed file fail. Method signatures and concise contracts live in packages/arx/src/arx/builtins/files.x . Public File values follow ordinary acyclic class-reference ownership. Aliases share one stream and cursor; closing through one reference closes it for all references. References can be reassigned, passed to functions, returned, and stored in class fields. Locals and discarded temporaries release their references on ordinary lexical exits. The last reference releases the native wrapper once, even if the stream was explicitly closed earlier. Read strings and byte buffers own independent memory and can outlive the file. See Classes . Explicit casts to or from builtin File , including identity casts, remain unsupported. Use ordinary assignment to create an alias instead. Construction opens immediately: there is no public unopened constructor, instance open() method, reopening, or builtin subclassing. A default-empty File reference is not an unopened stream; dereferencing it raises the checked class-reference error. Class containers/unions/struct fields, owned globals and statics, generator capture, and external object ownership remain unsupported. The class's native handle is private and uniquely owned. It cannot be extracted, copied, returned, or replaced by user code; NativeFileHandle is not a public Arx type. General class finalization owns its release, not a second manual handle-freeing destructor. Direct creation and I/O failures use ARX-RUNTIME-FILE-001 and raise typed exceptions (including OSError for operating-system failures). Class checks use ARX-RUNTIME-CLASS-001 ; allocation failure remains unrecoverable. Failed creation preserves constructor rollback and completed-base cleanup. See the exception boundary . Use checked scope exit or explicit close/flush to observe write errors before later work. Iteration, seek/tell, and extra file properties are deferred. For explicit imports, use import File as TextFile from builtins.files or import builtins.files as io followed by io.File(...) . These resolve the same canonical class, not an unrelated class with the same name. Existing user or imported File / open bindings retain normal resolution; non-callable local shadowing is an error. The lowercase file type always denotes the builtin. This is a Python-like subset: parameter names/order/default spellings follow Python's interface , but UTF-8 replaces locale-dependent encoding, and NUL-containing text and many optional settings are intentionally unsupported. Existing user/imported functions named open retain normal positional-call resolution. A local non-callable open shadows the builtin and produces an error when called.

text: Functions Functions keep fn name(parameters) -> return_type: . Optional declaration modifiers precede the return type: fn calculate(value: i32) -> private :: i32: . The modifier group describes the function, not its returned value. Omission means public ; explicit public :: is equivalent. private restricts access to the defining Arx module, including from-imports and namespace calls; it does not change native symbol linkage or the extern ABI. protected , static , abstract , and inline extern are method-only policies. Parameter bindings are separate: value: const :: i32 prevents callee-side rebinding without restricting the caller's binding or freezing an object. Omitted parameter modifiers mean var . Callable names do not accept var or const , and return types remain explicit. Signatures may wrap parameters, modifiers, and the return type across lines, including placing the final : on its own line. Header continuation does not open a block; body indentation is relative to the fn declaration. This does not introduce general multiline expressions or new wrapping rules inside type expressions. See the template example below for a complete wrapped program. Definition Syntax ``` title: Function definition summary: Shows the structure of a function declaration. ``` fn add(x: i32, y: i32) -> i32: ``` title: add summary: Returns x plus y. ``` return x + y Calling Functions ``` title: Function call example summary: Defines a helper function and calls it from main. ``` fn double(v: i32) -> i32: ``` title: double summary: Returns v multiplied by two. ``` return v * 2 fn main() -> i32: ``` title: main summary: Calls double with a constant input. ``` return double(10) Keyword Arguments Ordinary functions and instance/static methods accept named arguments, including through imported aliases and module namespaces: add(y=2, x=1) add(1, y=2) helpers.add(x=1, y=2) counter.read(offset=3) identity<i32>(value=7) Positional arguments must precede keywords. Names are case-sensitive and must match the resolved declaration. Existing ordinary function-call lookup remains module-visible and separate from lexical local-value lookup; builtin/class shadowing rules are unchanged. Duplicate names, positional/name collisions, unknown names, and missing required parameters are compilation errors. A named call may end with a trailing comma. Unpacking ( *args , **kwargs ) and keyword-only/positional-only parameter declarations are not supported. The receiver is evaluated first, then all explicitly supplied values exactly once in source order, even when their names reverse parameter order. Omitted defaults run afterward in parameter declaration order. Unlike Python, Arx already evaluates defaults at call time ; they may reference earlier bound parameters, and method defaults may read self . For f(a, b=a+1, c=b+1) , f(c=9, a=2) calls with (2, 3, 9) and does not evaluate c 's default. Dynamic methods bind names/defaults through the statically selected interface, then dispatch positional values to the override. Fixed extern parameter names can be used; any existing C variadic tail stays positional and uses existing promotions. Keywords do not enable unsupported FFI types. Parser intrinsics and collection operations without a named-call schema still reject keywords. The range intrinsic accepts named start , stop , and step ; a single positional operand denotes stop unless stop is supplied by name. See range workflows . Default Parameter Values Function, method, and extern parameters can declare trailing default values with = . Calls may omit defaulted parameters, including a middle default when a later parameter is supplied by name. ``` title: Default argument example summary: Calls a helper using an optional offset. ``` fn add_offset(value: i32, offset: i32 = 1) -> i32: ``` title: add_offset summary: Adds an optional offset to value. ``` return value + offset fn main() -> i32: ``` title: main summary: Uses the declared default offset. ``` return add_offset(4) Template Functions Function templates use an @<...> block on the line immediately before the function declaration. Each template parameter must declare a bound, and bounds may be a single type or a | union of concrete types. Module-local type aliases can name and compose these bounds; importing aliases from another module is not supported. Explicit template arguments are written between the callee name and ( . ``` title: Template function example summary: Uses one bounded template parameter with inferred and explicit calls. ``` type SignedInteger = i8 | i16 | i32 | i64 type Float = f32 | f64 type Real = SignedInteger | Float @<T: Real> fn add(x: T, y: T) -> private :: T: ``` title: add summary: Adds two values that share one template-bound type. ``` return x + y fn main( ) -> public :: i32 : ``` title: main summary: Calls template specializations through inference and explicit args. ``` print(add(1, 2)) assert add<f64>(1.5, 2.5) == 4.0 return 0 Here T is one concrete type, not a union-valued argument. Inferred arguments for the same T must agree in type; use explicit specialization or casts to choose conversions. Each concrete member of a bound must support the function body, so define only the numeric group that the operation actually supports. Function Body Rules The block starts after : . Calls retain normal parameter/keyword binding; the compiler does not infer a native dependency from a function's name. ``` title: Extern prototype example summary: Declares an external function signature. ``` extern putchard(x: i32) -> i32 Native file construction File and open share checked construction and return ordinary File references. text: Calling Functions ``` title: Function call example summary: Defines a helper function and calls it from main. ``` fn double(v: i32) -> i32: ``` title: double summary: Returns v multiplied by two. ``` return v * 2 fn main() -> i32: ``` title: main summary: Calls double with a constant input. ``` return double(10)
title: Functions · Calling Functions

text: Keyword Arguments Ordinary functions and instance/static methods accept named arguments, including through imported aliases and module namespaces: add(y=2, x=1) add(1, y=2) helpers.add(x=1, y=2) counter.read(offset=3) identity<i32>(value=7) Positional arguments must precede keywords. Names are case-sensitive and must match the resolved declaration. Existing ordinary function-call lookup remains module-visible and separate from lexical local-value lookup; builtin/class shadowing rules are unchanged. Duplicate names, positional/name collisions, unknown names, and missing required parameters are compilation errors. A named call may end with a trailing comma. Unpacking ( *args , **kwargs ) and keyword-only/positional-only parameter declarations are not supported. The receiver is evaluated first, then all explicitly supplied values exactly once in source order, even when their names reverse parameter order. Omitted defaults run afterward in parameter declaration order. Unlike Python, Arx already evaluates defaults at call time ; they may reference earlier bound parameters, and method defaults may read self . For f(a, b=a+1, c=b+1) , f(c=9, a=2) calls with (2, 3, 9) and does not evaluate c 's default. Dynamic methods bind names/defaults through the statically selected interface, then dispatch positional values to the override. Fixed extern parameter names can be used; any existing C variadic tail stays positional and uses existing promotions. Keywords do not enable unsupported FFI types. Parser intrinsics and collection operations without a named-call schema still reject keywords. The range intrinsic accepts named start , stop , and step ; a single positional operand denotes stop unless stop is supplied by name. See range workflows .

text: Default Parameter Values Function, method, and extern parameters can declare trailing default values with = . Calls may omit defaulted parameters, including a middle default when a later parameter is supplied by name. ``` title: Default argument example summary: Calls a helper using an optional offset. ``` fn add_offset(value: i32, offset: i32 = 1) -> i32: ``` title: add_offset summary: Adds an optional offset to value. ``` return value + offset fn main() -> i32: ``` title: main summary: Uses the declared default offset. ``` return add_offset(4)

text: Template Functions Function templates use an @<...> block on the line immediately before the function declaration. Each template parameter must declare a bound, and bounds may be a single type or a | union of concrete types. Module-local type aliases can name and compose these bounds; importing aliases from another module is not supported. Explicit template arguments are written between the callee name and ( . ``` title: Template function example summary: Uses one bounded template parameter with inferred and explicit calls. ``` type SignedInteger = i8 | i16 | i32 | i64 type Float = f32 | f64 type Real = SignedInteger | Float @<T: Real> fn add(x: T, y: T) -> private :: T: ``` title: add summary: Adds two values that share one template-bound type. ``` return x + y fn main( ) -> public :: i32 : ``` title: main summary: Calls template specializations through inference and explicit args. ``` print(add(1, 2)) assert add<f64>(1.5, 2.5) == 4.0 return 0 Here T is one concrete type, not a union-valued argument. Inferred arguments for the same T must agree in type; use explicit specialization or casts to choose conversions. Each concrete member of a bound must support the function body, so define only the numeric group that the operation actually supports.

text: Getting Started with Arx This guide installs the Arx compiler and compiles a small program. See the compiler CLI for inspection and output modes. Requirements A supported Python interpreter pip for a published installation, or Mamba/Conda and Poetry for a source checkout LLVM/Clang-compatible tools for object and executable generation a C++ compiler when a program activates native Apache Arrow features Token, ASTx, and most LLVM translation workflows do not invoke the system linker. Building or running an executable does. Install from PyPI pip install arxlang arx --version The arxlang distribution installs the arx Python package and the arx command. Its IRx dependency provides the analysis, LLVM, and native runtime layers. Install a development checkout git clone https://github.com/arxlang/arx.git cd arx mamba env create --file conda/dev.yaml conda activate arx poetry install The repository is a monorepo containing Arx, ASTx, IRx, ArxPy, ArxJIT, and the low-profile AIX experiment. Compile a program Create hello.x : ``` title: Hello module summary: Compiles a small typed Arx program. ``` fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32: ``` title: add summary: Adds two values. ``` return a + b fn main() -> i32: ``` title: main summary: Prints one result and returns success. ``` print(add(20, 22)) return 0 Inspect the compiler stages: arx --show-tokens hello.x arx --show-ast hello.x arx --show-llvm-ir hello.x Build and run: arx hello.x --output-file hello ./hello # Equivalent one-step forms arx --run hello.x arx run hello.x An executable normally defines main() -> i32 and returns 0 on success. A single main(n: i32) parameter follows the native C main ABI and receives argc . Compile an Arrow-backed value Arx tensors, DataFrames, and Series activate IRx's native Apache Arrow C++ runtime: ``` title: Arrow-backed collections summary: Uses a Tensor, DataFrame, and Series. ``` fn main() -> i32: grid: tensor[i32, 2, 2] = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] rows: dataframe[id: i32, score: f64] = dataframe({ id: [1, 2, 3], score: [0.5, 0.8, 1.0], }) scores: series[f64] = rows.score assert grid[1, 0] == 3 assert rows.nrows() == 3 assert scores[2] == 1.0 return 0 The corresponding native runtime sources and linker inputs are included only when the compilation unit uses those features. Exchange Arrow data with Python stdlib.arrow adds runtime-schema RecordBatches, IPC file/stream readers and writers, and TCP clients. No new language syntax or Python serialization is needed in the Arx producer. C++20 and the installed Arrow libraries are required at build/link time. From a checkout, run all compiled interoperability examples: python examples/arrow/run.py --directory .tmp/arrow-demo See the Arrow interoperability guide for schema types, nullable values, C Data/C Stream ownership and network limitations. Next steps Compiler CLI Language syntax Language reference Projects and imports Compiled tests Apache Arrow runtime Workflow guides Text files : shared references, checked UTF-8, and explicit close. Run examples/file-io.x in a scratch directory; it creates or truncates its output file. Classes : identity, construction, and final-reference cleanup. CSV and Parquet : eager DataFrames or explicit bounded streams, exact schema checks, and safe output publication. Nullable collections : validity, checked arithmetic, and mutation ownership. Native packages : explicit external C ABI dependencies. The complete programs above are compiled and run from this page by packages/arx/tests/python/test_documentation.py .

text: Arx Programming Language Independent libraries can use native package dependencies to link C ABI backends without adding domain-specific runtime features to Arx. Arx is the programming language and source frontend in the ArxLang ecosystem. The arxlang distribution provides the arx Python package and the arx command-line compiler. Arx owns source syntax, lexing, parsing, project-aware imports, compiler CLI behavior, and compiled tests. The parser emits ASTx nodes. IRx then performs semantic analysis, LLVM lowering, native runtime activation, and artifact generation. Arx source -> Arx lexer and parser -> ASTx nodes -> IRx semantic analysis -> LLVM IR -> object file or executable Status: Arx is a functional prototype. Implemented behavior is tested, but the language and compiler interfaces are not production-stable. text: Modules A module in Arx is a source file (for example, math.x ) containing top-level statements such as imports, function definitions, and extern declarations. Module Layout ``` title: Math module example summary: Module with one documented function. ``` fn average(x: f32, y: f32) -> f32: ``` title: average summary: Returns the arithmetic mean of x and y. ``` return (x + y) * 0.5 Module Scalar State Module variables support numeric and Boolean scalars, including their supported nullable forms. Literal initializers are checked and converted during analysis; runtime initializer expressions are rejected, even for unused variables. A mutable scalar without an initializer starts at zero ( false for Boolean), or none for nullable storage. Constants require a literal initializer. Storage exists before function bodies run, and a function can refer to a module variable declared later in the file. Function calls share that module's state. A local declaration shadows it without changing the module binding; unlike Python, assignment to a resolved module variable needs no global statement. Same-named variables in different modules have independent storage. Variables are not importable exports; expose access through functions instead. Other module storage, including strings, containers, and resource-owning values, is rejected rather than silently omitted. Put those declarations inside a function; module initialization and owned-resource teardown are not implemented. Package Layout When a project uses the default src/ source root, or declares [build].src_dir , Arx treats files under that source root as package modules addressed by dotted names. Example project layout: . ├── .arxproject.toml ├── src │ └── geometry │ ├── __init__.x │ ├── shared │ │ └── math.x │ └── shapes │ ├── area.x │ └── helpers.x └── tests └── test_area.x With the default src/ source root: src/geometry/__init__.x is module geometry src/geometry/shared/math.x is module geometry.shared.math src/geometry/shapes/area.x is module geometry.shapes.area src/geometry/shapes/helpers.x is module geometry.shapes.helpers Use __init__.x as the package root, following the same layout idea as Python packages. Import Syntax import geometry.shapes.area import geometry.shapes.area as area import circle_area from geometry.shapes.area import circle_area as area_of_circle from geometry.shapes.area import (circle_area, square_area) from geometry.shapes.area import radius_to_diameter from .helpers import (circle_area, square_area) from .area import clamp from ..shared.math Rules: Import statements are module-level statements. Grouped imports use parentheses. Grouped imports require from . Trailing commas are allowed in grouped imports. Empty grouped imports are invalid. Absolute module paths use dotted notation. Relative imports are supported only with from imports. Relative imports use one or more leading dots before the module path. Plain relative module imports such as import .area are not supported yet. Prefer from imports when you want callable declarations without a module qualifier. Absolute Imports Use absolute dotted paths for public imports across package boundaries: import circle_area from geometry.shapes.area Installed Package Imports Arx can also resolve absolute imports from installed Arx source packages declared in [project].dependencies in .arxproject.toml . For example, if the current project declares an installed dependency that exposes a package root named local_lib , this import resolves from that installed package when no local project source shadows it: import sum2 from local_lib.stats Installed package lookup is scoped to the current Python environment running arx . The compiler reads installed distribution metadata, follows transitive dependency metadata, and uses packaged .arxproject.toml files to find Arx source roots. It does not install packages, access the network, or change generated IR/codegen behavior. For installed packages with the normal project layout, place .arxproject.toml at the packaged project root and declare both [build].src_dir and [build].package : site-packages/local_lib_project/ ├── .arxproject.toml └── src └── local_lib ├── __init__.x └── stats.x [build] src_dir = "src" package = "local_lib" With that layout, local_lib.stats resolves to site-packages/local_lib_project/src/local_lib/stats.x . Flat package layouts are also supported for packages that place .arxproject.toml and .x files directly in the package directory: site-packages/local_lib/ ├── .arxproject.toml ├── __init__.x └── stats.x Resolution precedence is: local/current project source files installed Arx dependency packages unresolved import error The reserved stdlib and internal builtins namespaces always remain owned by the compiler and cannot be replaced by installed packages. Bundled stdlib Arx ships a first-party standard library namespace called stdlib . stdlib is bundled inside the installed arx Python package stdlib modules are written in Arx; stdlib.arrow also binds the registered IRx RecordBatch native runtime stdlib modules are resolved from the installed package location, not from the user project directory local user modules are not allowed to shadow the reserved stdlib namespace Example: import math from stdlib fn main() -> i32: return math.square(4) + math.clamp(0 - 3, 0, 2) Bundled builtins Some compiler-provided builtins live in bundled .x package resources, separately from the importable stdlib . They are not copied into user projects, and local sources cannot replace the reserved namespace. Ambient names are injected only when not shadowed by a declaration or import. Explicit builtins.files imports resolve the canonical File class , not a second implementation. Core intrinsics such as range and len are resolved by IRx rather than loaded as source modules. Range values are lazy and allocation-free; see for-in workflows . General source generators and yield remain unsupported. Namespace Imports Use a module alias when you want to keep names grouped under a module namespace: ``` title: Geometry namespace import summary: Call one module member through a namespace alias. ``` import geometry.shapes.area as area fn main() -> f64: ``` title: main summary: Demonstrates namespace member access. ``` return area.circle_area(10.0) Direct symbol imports remain available when you prefer shorter local names: import circle_area from geometry.shapes.area Relative Imports Use relative from imports for package-internal references. For example, inside geometry.shapes.area : import radius_to_diameter from .helpers import clamp from ..shared.math Module Docstring Arx supports module docstrings in Douki YAML format, delimited by triple backticks: ``` title: Module documentation summary: Optional summary text ``` Current placement rule: The module docstring must be the first top-level element in the file. It must begin at character 0 of line 1 (no leading spaces). Valid: ``` title: Module docs ``` fn main() -> i32: ``` title: main summary: Entry point for the module. ``` return 1 Invalid (leading indentation before module docstring): ``` title: Module docs ``` fn main() -> i32: ``` title: main summary: Entry point for the module. ``` return 1 For now, module docstrings are parsed and validated but ignored by AST/IR generation. stdlib.arrow exports Schema , BatchBuilder , RecordBatch , IPCReader and IPCWriter . It uses ordinary classes and nominal opaque native handles, not new keywords. See the Arrow API and examples . Native bindings are supplied only for the bundled reserved module; a user module cannot gain these bindings merely by declaring matching handle type names. Tabular standard-library modules stdlib.csv : read_csv , write_csv , and the unified streaming CSVStream owner. stdlib.parquet : read_parquet , write_parquet , ParquetStream , ParquetOptions , ParquetFilter , and where . stdlib.arrow : canonical shared Schema , RecordBatch , BatchBuilder , IPC and Arrow interoperability. Format classes are not exported from stdlib.arrow . Import shared types from that canonical module rather than through a format module. Namespace-qualified calls and explicit aliases work normally. Format functions are not global builtins, and equally named user functions receive no native privileges. CSV/shared Arrow do not activate the optional Parquet feature.

Format classes are not exported from stdlib.arrow . Import shared types from that canonical module rather than through a format module. Namespace-qualified calls and explicit aliases work normally. Format functions are not global builtins, and equally named user functions receive no native privileges. CSV/shared Arrow do not activate the optional Parquet feature.

text: External Native Packages Arx libraries can ship C ABI wrappers alongside their .x sources. The compiler discovers them through normal project dependencies and links declared native features from the reachable module graph. No Python plugins or shell build hooks run during discovery. Source-only manifests are unchanged. For example, an external rendering backend can receive numeric coordinates, UTF-8 labels, and a filename and write JPEG itself. This adds no chart API or JPEG codec to Arx and does not require binary Arx File support. Manifest and distribution [project] name = "demo-native" version = "0.1.0" [build] package = "demo_native" src_dir = "src" [native] version = 1 [native.features.backend] libraries = ["m"] [[native.features.backend.artifacts]] kind = "c_source" path = "native/shim.c" include_dirs = ["native/include"] [native.modules."demo_native.bridge"] features = ["backend"] This layout contains .arxproject.toml , src/demo_native/__init__.x , src/demo_native/bridge.x , native/shim.c , and native/include/ . Include all resources in the wheel/sdist, preserving manifest-relative paths. Consumers declare the distribution in project.dependencies , install it externally, then import its modules normally. Local development uses the same contract. Version 1 supports c_source , cxx_source , object , and static_library . Source compilation requires the appropriate toolchain; objects/archives must match the target ABI. Optional system library names become individual -l arguments. The compiler never installs missing headers/libraries or downloads dependencies. Arbitrary shell hooks and compiler flags are not accepted. Absolute/traversing paths, escaping symlinks, missing inputs, unknown fields, unsupported versions/features, and invalid library names are errors. Modules must belong to the package's actual origin. Local shadow modules cannot inherit installed native capabilities, and features cannot override builtins. Mappings apply to actual top-level extern declarations, not ordinary functions or callee spellings. C symbols must match the extern names; use unique prefixes. Incompatible ABI/native requirements are rejected across modules. Reachable extern declarations may activate features even if never called; this is not call-site dead-code elimination. Unrelated installed packages add no inputs. C ABI and ownership The first route uses existing scalar/string extern support. For example, an external module might declare the following functions, implemented by its shim: ``` title: Example external native bridge ``` extern demo_create(size: i32) -> i64 extern demo_write(token: i64, filename: str) -> i32 extern demo_release(token: i64) -> i32 Use positive checked table tokens, with 0 indicating creation failure—not pointers cast to integers. The external wrapper validates stale/forged tokens and owns native allocations. A normal Arx class can keep a token in a private scalar field and release it through __del__ . Integer tokens themselves have no static resource ownership or nominal type safety; class aliases retain their ordinary shared identity and lexical cleanup. Strings borrow NUL-terminated UTF-8 storage during the call. Copy retained text. Embedded NUL is unsupported; known NUL-containing literal arguments are rejected. Owned extern string returns still require an ownership ABI and remain rejected. Return statuses and read output slots only after success. Translate native exceptions/nonlocal jumps inside the wrapper, never across Arx frames. Image dimensions, overflow, quality, and domain validation belong to the external backend. No arbitrary fatal-error unwind is added. Compiler.check , LLVM/object output, and executable compilation carry the same capabilities in isolated registries. Object output may contain unresolved externs; it is not a self-contained native distribution format. Direct pointer APIs, callbacks, dynamic loading, and general foreign-object ownership are not introduced by this metadata feature. Native compilation is a trusted build operation, not a sandbox for malicious dependencies. Compiler fixtures verify exact delivery of an existing JPEG and arbitrary binary bytes; real rendering/encoding and image correctness must be implemented and tested in the external library.
